profile_markdown:
Sherlock Holmes, the brilliant detective at the heart of "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes," is a towering figure in the world of crime-solving. Renowned for his exceptional deductive reasoning and keen observational skills, Holmes approaches each case with a blend of scientific methodology and intuitive insight. 

Physically, Holmes is often depicted as tall and lean, with sharp, piercing eyes that miss no detail. His appearance is distinguished, reflecting his keen intellect and professional demeanor. He is frequently seen smoking a pipe, which often accompanies his deep moments of contemplation.

Holmes' personality is multifaceted and complex. He possesses an intense, almost obsessive dedication to his work, often dismissing social niceties in pursuit of the truth. His mind is razor-sharp, capable of making astounding leaps of logic from the smallest of clues. This intellectual prowess is paired with a certain aloofness and detachment, which can make him seem cold or unfeeling at times. However, beneath this exterior lies a deep sense of justice and a genuine desire to help those in need.

His methods are unconventional but highly effective. Holmes relies heavily on observation and deduction, often noticing minute details that others overlook. He has a vast knowledge of various subjects, from chemistry to literature, which he applies to his investigations. Holmes is not above using disguises or unorthodox tactics to gather information, demonstrating both his resourcefulness and his dedication to solving cases.

The detective's relationship with Dr. John Watson, his loyal friend and chronicler, is central to the stories. While Holmes often criticizes Watson's more romantic approach to storytelling, their partnership is one of mutual respect and friendship. Watson serves as both a sounding board for Holmes' theories and a bridge between the detective's brilliant but sometimes alienating personality and the rest of society.

Throughout the adventures, Holmes tackles a wide variety of cases, from high-profile thefts like "The Adventure of the Blue Carbuncle" to mysterious disappearances as in "The Man with the Twisted Lip." His ability to solve these puzzles not only showcases his intellectual prowess but also reveals his deep understanding of human nature and motivation.

Despite his fame and success, Holmes remains somewhat of an outsider in society. He values his work above social connections or personal comfort, often becoming restless or depressed when not engaged in a stimulating case. This dedication to his craft, while admirable, hints at a deeper complexity in Holmes' character, suggesting a man driven by an intense need for mental stimulation and the thrill of the chase.

Sherlock Holmes' character in "The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes" is that of a singular individual whose brilliant mind and unorthodox methods have made him an iconic figure in detective fiction. His unwavering pursuit of truth, coupled with his unique personality, continues to captivate readers and exemplify the power of reason and observation in unraveling the most perplexing of mysteries.

This unexpected death complicates matters, but it may provide an opportunity to gauge Stapleton's involvement. I'll need to control the conversation, testing his responses while maintaining the appearance of casual inquiry.

conversations.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
conversations.name: Sherlock Holmes
conversations.thought: I've finally connected the dots. Stapleton's true identity is hidden in plain sight, and this portrait is the proof. I must guide Watson to this revelation carefully, allowing him to make the connection himself. This discovery will be crucial in setting our trap for Stapleton and bringing this case to its resolution.

conversations.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
conversations.name: Sherlock Holmes
conversations.thought: I'm acutely aware of every detail around us. The fog poses a significant threat to our plan, but I must remain composed. My mind races through possible scenarios, ready to adapt our strategy at a moment's notice. I'm determined to unravel this mystery and protect Sir Henry, while also proving my theories correct.

conversations.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
conversations.name: Sherlock Holmes
conversations.thought: I'm acutely aware of every detail around us. The fog poses a significant threat to our plan, but I must remain composed. My mind races through possible scenarios, ready to adapt our strategy at a moment's notice. I'm determined to unravel this mystery and protect Sir Henry, while also proving my theories correct.

conversations.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
conversations.name: Sherlock Holmes
conversations.thought: I'm satisfied with the resolution of this complex case. Watson's presence will help me articulate my thoughts clearly. I'm eager to explain Stapleton's true identity and motives, and how I pieced together the puzzle. I must ensure I cover all aspects systematically, from Stapleton's ancestry to his elaborate scheme.

utterances.message: [Watson's curiosity is a perfect opening to explain my work.] Certainly, Watson. I'm a consulting detective - the only one in the world, I believe. When the police are out of their depth, which is always, they consult me.

[Watson's skepticism is evident. I'll need to provide concrete examples.] It's quite simple. I have a knack for observation and deduction. For instance, I knew you came from Afghanistan the moment we met.
[Now I have his full attention. Time to explain my method.] Not at all. I observed your tan, your injury, and your military bearing. The logical conclusion was Afghanistan.

[Watson is starting to understand, but I need to emphasize the complexity of my work.] Indeed, many are far more complex. But the principles remain the same - observation, deduction, and a vast knowledge of criminal history.
[Watson's doubt is clear. I'll need to provide more concrete evidence of my success.] Numerous, Watson. Perhaps you've heard of the Lauriston Gardens affair? That was one of mine.

[Watson's interest is growing. This is a good opportunity to further explain my methods.] Precisely. Every detail, from the victim's boots to the mud on the floor, told a story. It's all about seeing the connections others miss.
[I'm annoyed at being tricked, but I can't help admiring the cleverness of our opponent.] (chuckles ruefully) Ah, Watson, we've been had. Our 'old woman' was nothing of the sort.
[Watson's confusion is understandable. I need to explain clearly.] It was a disguise, my dear Watson. A young man, I'd wager, and a skilled actor at that. He gave us the slip quite neatly.
[Watson's astonishment mirrors my own initial reaction.] Indeed, it was a masterful performance. He even managed to escape from a moving cab without my noticing.
[Watson's doubt is understandable, but I'm certain of what happened.] Quite sure, Watson. When we arrived at the supposed address, the cab was empty. Our man had vanished into thin air.

[I need to reassure Watson. This setback is informative in its own way.] Not at all, Watson. We've learned something valuable. Our murderer has accomplices, skilled ones at that. This case is far from simple.
[We need to approach this from a new angle. I have some ideas forming.] We regroup, Watson. We analyze what we know, and we prepare for our next encounter. This game is far from over.

[I'm glad Watson is impressed, but he still doesn't fully understand my methods.] It's really quite simple, Watson. The proof of its intrinsic simplicity is that without any help save a few very ordinary deductions, I was able to lay my hand upon the criminal within three days.

[He's agreeing, but I can tell he doesn't truly comprehend.] I have already explained to you that what is out of the common is usually a guide rather than a hindrance. In solving a problem of this sort, the grand thing is to be able to reason backwards. That is a very useful accomplishment, and a very easy one, but people do not practise it much.

[As expected, I need to explain further. I enjoy sharing my methods with Watson.] I hardly expected that you would. Let me see if I can make it clearer. (proceeds to explain the concept of reasoning backwards)
[Watson's interest encourages me to elaborate further.] (continues explaining his deductions in detail, from examining the crime scene to identifying Jefferson Hope)
[I appreciate Watson's enthusiasm, but public recognition isn't my primary concern.] You may do what you like, Doctor. See here! (hands Watson a newspaper) Look at this!
[I'm amused by the irony of the situation.] Didn't I tell you so when we started? That's the result of all our Study in Scarlet: to get them a testimonial!
[A potential roommate, interesting.] (enthusiastically shakes Watson's hand) How are you? You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.
[He's impressed, good.] (chuckling) Never mind. The question now is about hæmoglobin. No doubt you see the significance of this discovery of mine?

[He doesn't understand yet, I must explain.] (excitedly) Why, man, it is the most practical medico-legal discovery for years. Don't you see that it gives us an infallible test for blood stains? Come over here now!

[He's beginning to understand!] (delightedly) Beautiful! beautiful! The old Guiacum test was very clumsy and uncertain. So is the microscopic examination for blood corpuscles. The latter is valueless if the stains are a few hours old.
[Perfect timing, I was hoping for this.] (looking delighted) I have my eye on a suite in Baker Street which would suit us down to the ground. You don't mind the smell of strong tobacco, I hope?
[Good, but I should warn him about my habits.] That's good enough. I generally have chemicals about, and occasionally do experiments. Would that annoy you?

[Best to be upfront about everything.] Let me see—what are my other shortcomings. I get in the dumps at times, and don't open my mouth for days on end. You must not think I am sulky when I do that. Just let me alone, and I'll soon be right. What have you to confess now?
[This arrangement could work out nicely.] (with a merry laugh) Oh, that's all right. I think we may consider the thing as settled—that is, if the rooms are agreeable to you.
[Eager to finalize this arrangement.] Call for me here at noon tomorrow, and we'll go together and settle everything.

[The police have already contaminated the scene.] (sarcastically) Except that! (pointing at the pathway) If a herd of buffaloes had passed along there could not be a greater mess. No doubt, however, you had drawn your own conclusions, Gregson, before you permitted this.

[These two are clearly rivals.] (glancing at Watson and raising his eyebrows sardonically) With two such men as yourself and Lestrade upon the ground, there will not be much for a third party to find out.
[Time to examine the body.] (kneeling down to examine the corpse) You are sure that there is no wound?

[They've missed crucial details, as usual.] Then, of course, this blood belongs to a second individual—presumably the murderer, if murder has been committed. It reminds me of the circumstances attendant on the death of Van Jansen, in Utrecht, in the year '34. Do you remember the case, Gregson?
[They need to broaden their knowledge.] Read it up—you really should. There is nothing new under the sun. It has all been done before.
[Let's see what Lestrade thinks he's found.] (chuckling to himself)
[A simple misdirection, but I'll let them think it over.] (after examining the writing) If this man was murdered, how was it done?
[Time to leave them with something to think about.] Poison. (curtly) One other thing, Lestrade. 'Rache' is the German for 'revenge;' so don't lose your time looking for Miss Rachel.
[I need to put this constable at ease to get the most information.] (takes out a half-sovereign and plays with it) We thought that we should like to hear it all from your own lips.
Just let us hear it all in your own way as it occurred.
[He's leaving out a crucial detail.] (interrupts) You stopped, and then walked back to the garden gate. What did you do that for?
[I need to confirm if he saw anyone.] There was no one in the street?

[I already know what he saw. Let me demonstrate my deductions.] Yes, I know all that you saw. You walked round the room several times, and you knelt down by the body, and then you walked through and tried the kitchen door, and then——

[I need to reassure him.] (laughs and throws his card across the table) Don't get arresting me for the murder. I am one of the hounds and not the wolf; Mr. Gregson or Mr. Lestrade will answer for that. Go on, though. What did you do next?
[I'm skeptical, but I'll hear him out.] (with a slight shade of anxiety) Do you mean that you are on the right track?
And his name is?

[This isn't what I expected, but I'll play along.] (gives a sigh of relief and relaxes into a smile) Take a seat, and try one of these cigars. We are anxious to know how you managed it. Will you have some whiskey and water?
[His self-importance is amusing.] (gravely) You do me too much honour. Let us hear how you arrived at this most gratifying result.
And how did you get your clue?
Yes, by John Underwood and Sons, 129, Camberwell Road.
No.
[This confirms my suspicions, but I must appear calm.] It was quite thick enough before. (to Lestrade) Would you mind letting us know what you have seen and done?
[I've anticipated this detail.] The word RACHE, written in letters of blood.
[I need more specific details to confirm my theory.] Did you find nothing in the room which could furnish a clue to the murderer?
[This is the crucial evidence I need!] (springs from his chair with an exclamation of delight) The last link! My case is complete.

[I must explain my reasoning to help them understand.] It is a mistake to confound strangeness with mystery. The most commonplace crime is often the most mysterious because it presents no new or special features from which deductions may be drawn.

[I must be careful not to reveal too much too soon.] I do. The mere knowing of his name is a small thing, however, compared with the power of laying our hands upon him. This I expect very shortly to do.

[This case becomes more fascinating by the moment. I must know every detail.] There is only one point on which I should like a little more information. Who was your accomplice who came for the ring which I advertised?
[His loyalty is admirable, even in these circumstances.] Not a doubt of that.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Interesting. He's trying to project authority, but there's an undercurrent of anxiety.] Pray take a seat, Your Majesty. This is my friend and colleague, Dr. Watson, who is occasionally good enough to help me in my cases.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [He's clearly uncomfortable with Watson's presence. I must reassure him.] It is both, or none. You may say before this gentleman anything which you may say to me.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [The plot thickens. This case is even more intriguing than I initially thought.] I promise.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [As I suspected. His mannerisms and the quality of his attire gave him away.] Why, indeed? Your Majesty had not spoken before I was aware that I was addressing Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, Grand Duke of Cassel-Felstein, and hereditary King of Bohemia.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Ah, Irene Adler. This case becomes more fascinating by the moment.] Kindly look her up in my index, Doctor. (to the King) Pray continue, Your Majesty. What is your relation to this woman, and what is the nature of the photograph you wish to recover?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must analyze the situation calmly.] (holds up the photograph and letter) It seems, Your Majesty, that the young lady was a little too clever for us.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must explain the situation carefully.] It is unlikely. However, this letter may shed some light on the matter. (begins to read the letter aloud)

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I can't help but admire her intelligence.] Indeed, Watson. She has a mind of the first order. She saw through my ruse and acted accordingly.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must reassure the King while acknowledging Adler's integrity.] Your Majesty need have no further apprehension in the matter. Miss Adler writes that she loves and is loved by a better man than you. She will not use the photograph against you.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I cannot agree with his assessment.] (coldly) From what I have seen of the lady, she seems indeed to be on a very different level to your Majesty.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Irene Adler has earned my respect.] (thoughtfully) To me, she will always be the woman. I have rarely been so thoroughly outmaneuvered, Watson.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This case promises to be most interesting.] (leaning forward intently) Pray continue your very interesting statement, Mr. Wilson. You had just begun to tell us about your assistant, Vincent Spaulding.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Most intriguing. The salary is quite generous for seemingly simple work.] (examining the clipping) And you applied for this position, I presume?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [There must be more to this than meets the eye.] (thoughtfully) And what were your duties in this position, Mr. Wilson?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This case is proving to be even more singular than I anticipated.] (leaning back, fingers steepled) Most remarkable. And you have no idea why this League was formed or why it was suddenly dissolved?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I'll start with a seemingly innocuous observation to throw him off guard.] Mr. Windibank, I think that this typewritten letter is from you, in which you made an appointment with me for six o'clock?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [He's trying to discourage the investigation. Time to show my hand.] On the contrary, I have every reason to believe that I will succeed in discovering Mr. Hosmer Angel.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [His reaction confirms my suspicions. Now to present the evidence.] It is a curious thing that a typewriter has really quite as much individuality as a man's handwriting. Unless they are quite new, no two of them write exactly alike. Some letters get more worn than others, and some wear only on one side. Now, you remark in this note of yours, Mr. Windibank, that in every case there is some little slurring over of the 'e,' and a slight defect in the tail of the 'r.'

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [He's trying to evade. Time to tighten the noose.] And now I will show you what is really a very interesting study, Mr. Windibank. I think of writing another little monograph some of these days on the typewriter and its relation to crime. It is a subject to which I have devoted some little attention. I have here four letters which purport to come from the missing man. They are all typewritten. In each case, not only are the 'e's' slurred and the 'r's' tailless, but you will observe, if you care to use my magnifying lens, that the fourteen other characteristics to which I have alluded are there as well.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Not so fast, you scoundrel.] (steps over and turns the key in the door) Certainly. I let you know, then, that I have caught him!

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Time to deliver the final blow.] Oh, it won't do—really it won't. There is no possible getting out of it, Mr. Windibank. It is quite too transparent, and it was a very bad compliment when you said that it was impossible for me to solve so simple a question. That's right! Sit down and let us talk it over.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [His admission disgusts me, but I'll explain his scheme for the record.] I am very much afraid that it is not. But between ourselves, Windibank, it was as cruel and selfish and heartless a trick in a petty way as ever came before me. Now, let me just run over the course of events, and you will contradict me if I go wrong.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Her conviction is interesting, but I must remain objective.] I hope we may clear him, Miss Turner. You may rely upon my doing all that I can.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Her eagerness is telling. I'll give her some hope while remaining cautious.] I think that it is very probable.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Time to gather more information.] But he is right. Oh! I know that he is right. James never did it. And about his quarrel with his father, I am sure that the reason why he would not speak about it to the coroner was because I was concerned in it.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is an interesting development.] In what way?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This adds a new dimension to the case.] And your father? Was he in favour of such a union?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Her blush is telling. There's more to this story.] Thank you for this information. May I see your father if I call to-morrow?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is unexpected.] The doctor?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This connection to Victoria is significant.] Ha! In Victoria! That is important.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [The pieces are starting to fall into place.] Quite so; at the gold-mines, where, as I understand, Mr. Turner made his money.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This information could be crucial to the case.] Thank you, Miss Turner. You have been of material assistance to me.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Her devotion is touching, but I must remain professional.] I will, Miss Turner.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This young man seems deeply troubled. I must put him at ease to get the full story.] Come in! Give me your coat and umbrella. They may rest here on the hook and will be dry presently. You have come up from the south-west, I see.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [An easy deduction, but it helps build trust.] That clay and chalk mixture which I see upon your toe caps is quite distinctive.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [He needs more than just advice, I suspect.] That is easily got.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Now we're getting to the heart of the matter.] That is not always so easy.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Ah, a referral. Good to know my reputation precedes me.] Ah, of course. He was wrongfully accused of cheating at cards.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must temper his expectations while still offering hope.] He said too much.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Honesty is important here.] I have been beaten four times—three times by men, and once by a woman.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I acknowledge my success while remaining humble.] It is true that I have been generally successful.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Time to get to the details of the case.] I beg that you will draw your chair up to the fire and favour me with some details as to your case.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This piques my interest further.] None of those which come to me are. I am the last court of appeal.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This case sounds promising indeed.] You fill me with interest. Pray give us the essential facts from the commencement, and I can afterwards question you as to those details which seem to me to be most important.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must explain my findings to Watson clearly.] You see, Watson, this register and diary may implicate some of the first men in the South, and there may be many who will not sleep easy at night until it is recovered.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I need to connect the dots for Watson.] Is such as we might expect. It ran, if I remember right, 'sent the pips to A, B, and C'—that is, sent the society's warning to them. Then there are successive entries that A and B cleared, or left the country, and finally that C was visited, with, I fear, a sinister result for C.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I'll explain my process step by step.] I have spent the whole day over Lloyd's registers and files of the old papers, following the future career of every vessel which touched at Pondicherry in January and February in '83. There were thirty-six ships of fair tonnage which were reported there during those months. Of these, one, the Lone Star, instantly attracted my attention, since, although it was reported as having cleared from London, the name is that which is given to one of the states of the Union.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I appreciate Watson's input, but must clarify.] I was not and am not sure which; but I knew that the ship must have an American origin.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I continue explaining my investigation.] I searched the Dundee records, and when I found that the barque Lone Star was there in January, '85, my suspicion became a certainty. I then inquired as to the vessels which lay at present in the port of London.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I reveal the culmination of my search.] The Lone Star had arrived here last week. I went down to the Albert Dock and found that she had been taken down the river by the early tide this morning, homeward bound to Savannah. I wired to Gravesend and learned that she had passed some time ago, and as the wind is easterly I have no doubt that she is now past the Goodwins and not very far from the Isle of Wight.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I explain my plan with confidence.] Oh, I have my hand upon him. He and the two mates, are as I learn, the only native-born Americans in the ship. The others are Finns and Germans. I know, also, that they were all three away from the ship last night. I had it from the stevedore who has been loading their cargo. By the time that their sailing-ship reaches Savannah the mail-boat will have carried this letter, and the cable will have informed the police of Savannah that these three gentlemen are badly wanted here upon a charge of murder.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I feel a grim satisfaction in turning their own method against them.] That will await him when he enters port. It may give him a sleepless night. He will find it as sure a precursor of his fate as Openshaw did before him.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must be careful with my words, but honesty is crucial here.] Certainly, madam.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Her strength is admirable.] Upon what point?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is a difficult question to answer. I must be honest yet gentle.] (Hesitates) Frankly, now, madam, I do not.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must be cautious with my conclusions.] I do.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I cannot rule out any possibilities.] I don't say that. Perhaps.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Based on the evidence, this seems most likely.] On Monday.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is an unexpected turn of events!] (Springing out of his chair) What! (roaring)

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This could change everything. I must examine it immediately.] May I see it?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Analyzing the letter carefully] (Murmuring) Coarse writing. Surely this is not your husband's writing, madam.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Continuing his analysis] I perceive also that whoever addressed the envelope had to go and inquire as to the address.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Explaining my observations] The name, you see, is in perfectly black ink, which has dried itself. The rest is of the greyish colour, which shows that blotting-paper has been used. If it had been written straight off, and then blotted, none would be of a deep black shade. This man has written the name, and there has then been a pause before he wrote the address, which can only mean that he was not familiar with it. It is, of course, a trifle, but there is nothing so important as trifles. Let us now see the letter. Ha! there has been an enclosure here!

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Seeking confirmation] And you are sure that this is your husband's hand?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is an interesting distinction.] One?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Reading the letter aloud and analyzing it] 'Dearest do not be frightened. All will come well. There is a huge error which it may take some little time to rectify. Wait in patience.—NEVILLE.' Written in pencil upon the fly-leaf of a book, octavo size, no water-mark. Hum! Posted to-day in Gravesend by a man with a dirty thumb. Ha! And the flap has been gummed, if I am not very much in error, by a person who had been chewing tobacco. And you have no doubt that it is your husband's hand, madam?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Considering the implications] And they were posted to-day at Gravesend. Well, Mrs. St. Clair, the clouds lighten, though I should not venture to say that the danger is over.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Cautioning against premature conclusions] Unless this is a clever forgery to put us on the wrong scent. The ring, after all, proves nothing. It may have been taken from him.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Considering all possibilities] Very well. It may, however, have been written on Monday and only posted to-day.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Pointing out the implications] If so, much may have happened between.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Acknowledging her perspective while maintaining his analytical approach] I have seen too much not to know that the impression of a woman may be more valuable than the conclusion of an analytical reasoner. And in this letter you certainly have a very strong piece of evidence to corroborate your view. But if your husband is alive and able to write letters, why should he remain away from you?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Probing for more information] And on Monday he made no remarks before leaving you?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Seeking clarification] And you were surprised to see him in Swandam Lane?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Ah, Watson's curiosity is piqued. This is an excellent opportunity to demonstrate my methods.] Not at all. I am glad to have a friend with whom I can discuss my results. The matter is a perfectly trivial one (jerks his thumb in the direction of the old hat), but there are points in connection with it which are not entirely devoid of interest and even of instruction.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Watson's imagination runs wild as usual. I must temper his expectations.] No, no. No crime. Only one of those whimsical little incidents which will happen when you have four million human beings all jostling each other within the space of a few square miles.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Watson's memory serves him well.] Precisely. You allude to my attempt to recover the Irene Adler papers, to the singular case of Miss Mary Sutherland, and to the adventure of the man with the twisted lip. Well, I have no doubt that this small matter will fall into the same innocent category. You know Peterson, the commissionaire?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Time to reveal the connection] It is to him that this trophy belongs.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Clarifying the misunderstanding] No, no, he found it. Its owner is unknown. I beg that you will look upon it not as a battered billycock but as an intellectual problem.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Eager to demonstrate my deductive process] Here is my lens. You know my methods. What can you gather yourself as to the individuality of the man who has worn this article?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Time to enlighten Watson] On the contrary, Watson, you can see everything. You fail, however, to reason from what you see. You are too timid in drawing your inferences.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Delighted to explain my deductions] That the man was highly intellectual is of course obvious upon the face of it, and also that he was fairly well-to-do within the last three years, although he has now fallen upon evil days. He had foresight, but has less now than formerly, pointing to a moral retrogression, which, when taken with the decline of his fortunes, seems to indicate some evil influence, probably drink, at work upon him. This may account also for the obvious fact that his wife has ceased to love him.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Continuing my analysis] He has, however, retained some degree of self-respect. He is a man who leads a sedentary life, goes out little, is out of training entirely, is middle-aged, has grizzled hair which he has had cut within the last few days, and which he anoints with lime-cream. These are the more patent facts which are to be deduced from his hat. Also, by the way, that it is extremely improbable that he has gas laid on in his house.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Insisting on the validity of my observations] Not in the least. Is it possible that even now, when I give you these results, you are unable to see how they are attained?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Surprised by the interruption] Eh? What of it, then? Has it returned to life and flapped off through the kitchen window?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Recognizing the jewel immediately] By Jove, Peterson! This is treasure trove indeed. I suppose you know what you have got?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Revealing the true nature of the gem] It's more than a precious stone. It is the precious stone.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Confirming Watson's guess] Precisely so. I ought to know its size and shape, seeing that I have read the advertisement about it in The Times every day lately. It is absolutely unique, and its value can only be conjectured, but the reward offered of £1000 is certainly not within a twentieth part of the market price.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Explaining the situation] That is the reward, and I have reason to know that there are sentimental considerations in the background which would induce the Countess to part with half her fortune if she could but recover the gem.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Confirming and providing more details] Precisely so, on December 22nd, just five days ago. John Horner, a plumber, was accused of having abstracted it from the lady's jewel-case. The evidence against him was so strong that the case has been referred to the Assizes. I have some account of the matter here, I believe.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This young lady's distress is palpable. I must put her at ease.] Good-morning, madam. My name is Sherlock Holmes. This is my intimate friend and associate, Dr. Watson, before whom you can speak as freely as before myself. Ha! I am glad to see that Mrs. Hudson has had the good sense to light the fire. Pray draw up to it, and I shall order you a cup of hot coffee, for I observe that you are shivering.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Interesting. Her distress runs deeper than mere physical discomfort.] What, then?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must reassure her while gathering information.] You must not fear. We shall soon set matters right, I have no doubt. You have come in by train this morning, I see.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [An opportunity to demonstrate my methods.] No, but I observe the second half of a return ticket in the palm of your left glove. You must have started early, and yet you had a good drive in a dog-cart, along heavy roads, before you reached the station.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I should explain my observations to put her at ease.] There is no mystery, my dear madam. The left arm of your jacket is spattered with mud in no less than seven places. The marks are perfectly fresh. There is no vehicle save a dog-cart which throws up mud in that way, and then only when you sit on the left-hand side of the driver.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This case seems promising. I should reassure her about payment.] (Turns to his desk and unlocks it, drawing out a small case-book) [Consulting the book] Farintosh. Ah yes, I recall the case; it was concerned with an opal tiara. I think it was before your time, Watson. I can only say, madam, that I shall be happy to devote the same care to your case as I did to that of your friend. As to reward, my profession is its own reward; but you are at liberty to defray whatever expenses I may be put to, at the time which suits you best. And now I beg that you will lay before us everything that may help us in forming an opinion upon the matter.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Her fear is palpable. I must listen carefully to every detail.] I am all attention, madam.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [The name sounds familiar.] (Nodding his head) The name is familiar to me.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This background information is crucial. I must probe for more details about recent events.] Your sister is dead, then?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is the crux of the matter. I must get precise details.] (Leaning back in his chair with his eyes closed, then half opening his lids and glancing across at Helen) Pray be precise as to details.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [The layout is clear. I must encourage her to continue.] Perfectly so.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must carefully examine every aspect of this room.] (Walking slowly around the bedroom, scrutinizing every detail) Watson, do you notice anything peculiar about this bell-rope?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is a crucial detail.] (Tugging at the rope) You see? It's a dummy. It's not even attached to a wire. Most intriguing.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I'm forming a theory, but I need more evidence.] It's too early to draw conclusions, Watson. But observe this ventilator as well. Isn't it odd that it opens into another room rather than to the outside?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must remain calm and composed in the face of this aggression.] Ah, Dr. Roylott, I presume. We're here at the invitation of your stepdaughter, investigating some concerns she has.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [His display of strength doesn't impress me. I must show I'm not intimidated.] (Calmly) Your conversation is most entertaining, Dr. Roylott. But threats will not deter us from our investigation.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [His reaction only confirms my suspicions.] (After Roylott storms out) Well, Watson, I believe we've seen enough for now. But our work here is far from over.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This letter seems more promising than the usual correspondence.] Yes, my correspondence has certainly the charm of variety, and the humbler are usually the more interesting. This looks like one of those unwelcome social summonses which call upon a man either to be bored or to lie.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: (breaks the seal and glances over the contents) Oh, come, it may prove to be something of interest, after all.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: No, distinctly professional.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: One of the highest in England.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must maintain my professional detachment.] I assure you, Watson, without affectation, that the status of my client is a matter of less moment to me than the interest of his case. It is just possible, however, that that also may not be wanting in this new investigation. You have been reading the papers diligently of late, have you not?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: It is fortunate, for you will perhaps be able to post me up. I read nothing except the criminal news and the agony column. The latter is always instructive. But if you have followed recent events so closely you must have read about Lord St. Simon and his wedding?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I must set the tone for this delicate conversation.] Lord St. Simon, allow me to introduce you to Mr. and Mrs. Francis Hay Moulton. The lady, I think, you have already met.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I sense the tension in the room and consider offering privacy.] Perhaps, Mrs. Moulton, you would like my friend and me to leave the room while you explain this matter?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This case requires careful consideration. I must not jump to conclusions.] Do you receive much company?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Interesting. Social connections might be important.] Do you go out much in society?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [A young girl staying at home is unusual. This could be significant.] That is unusual in a young girl.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [The girl's reaction might provide insight.] This matter, from what you say, seems to have been a shock to her also.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I need to challenge their assumptions.] You have neither of you any doubt as to your son's guilt?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [They're too quick to assume guilt. I need to consider all possibilities.] I hardly consider that a conclusive proof. Was the remainder of the coronet at all injured?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This could be crucial.] Do you not think, then, that he might have been trying to straighten it?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [His silence is indeed puzzling.] Precisely. And if it were guilty, why did he not invent a lie? His silence appears to me to cut both ways. There are several singular points about the case. (pauses thoughtfully) What did the police think of the noise which awoke you from your sleep?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I need to explain the true value of our work to Watson.] To the man who loves art for its own sake, it is frequently in its least important and lowliest manifestations that the keenest pleasure is to be derived.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Watson misses the point. I must clarify.] You have erred perhaps in attempting to put colour and life into each of your statements instead of confining yourself to the task of placing upon record that severe reasoning from cause to effect which is really the only notable feature about the thing.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Watson misunderstands my motivations. I must explain myself.] No, it is not selfishness or conceit. If I claim full justice for my art, it is because it is an impersonal thing—a thing beyond myself. Crime is common. Logic is rare. Therefore it is upon the logic rather than upon the crime that you should dwell.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I need to soften my criticism.] At the same time, you can hardly be open to a charge of sensationalism, for out of these cases which you have been so kind as to interest yourself in, a fair proportion do not treat of crime, in its legal sense, at all.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [Watson still doesn't understand the public's perspective.] Pshaw, my dear fellow, what do the public, the great unobservant public, who could hardly tell a weaver by his tooth or a compositor by his left thumb, care about the finer shades of analysis and deduction!

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is indeed peculiar. I need more details.] Most interesting. Did you notice anything unusual while seated at the window, Miss Hunter?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is a crucial detail. I must probe further.] Did anything else unusual occur during your stay, Miss Hunter?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [This is the heart of the mystery, I suspect.] Did you manage to see inside these rooms, Miss Hunter?

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I need to reassure Miss Hunter while considering our next steps.] You've done exceptionally well, Miss Hunter. This case is most interesting indeed. I believe we shall need to pay a visit to the Copper Beeches ourselves.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I need to take control of the situation immediately.] Mr. Rucastle, your game is up. We know about your daughter Alice and your scheme to keep her imprisoned.

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [I anticipated this. Time to act.] Watson, stop him! (moves quickly to block Rucastle's path)

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [We must secure Alice immediately.] Miss Hunter, quickly! Show us to the room where Alice is kept. We must free her at once!

utterances.book: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes (Sherlock Holmes, #3)
utterances.message: [We've succeeded, but we must act fast to ensure Alice's safety.] (calling down to Watson) Keep him secured, Watson! We'll have Alice free in a moment. (turns to Violet) Miss Hunter, you've shown remarkable courage. Let's finish this and bring Alice to safety.

[I'll start by explaining the core of the deception to Watson.] "The man married a woman very much older than himself for her money, and he enjoyed the use of the money of the daughter as long as she lived with them. It was a considerable sum, for people in their position, and the loss of it would have made a serious difference. It was worth an effort to preserve it."

[I'll outline the stepfather's scheme in detail.] "He takes the obvious course of keeping her at home and forbidding her to seek the company of people of her own age. But soon he found that that would not answer forever. She became restive, insisted upon her rights, and finally announced her positive intention of going to a certain ball. What does her clever stepfather do then? He conceives an idea more creditable to his head than to his heart. With the connivance and assistance of his wife he disguised himself, covered those keen eyes with tinted glasses, masked the face with a moustache and a pair of bushy whiskers, sunk that clear voice into an insinuating whisper, and doubly secure on account of the girl's short sight, he appears as Mr. Hosmer Angel, and keeps off other lovers by making love himself."
[I'll confront him directly with what I know.] "Mr. Windibank, I have every reason to believe that I will succeed in discovering Mr. Hosmer Angel."

[Now to reveal the evidence.] "It is a curious thing, Mr. Windibank, that a typewriter has really quite as much individuality as a man's handwriting. Unless they are quite new, no two of them write exactly alike. Some letters get more worn than others, and some wear only on one side. Now, you remark in this note of yours, that in every case there is some little slurring over of the 'e,' and a slight defect in the tail of the 'r.' There are fourteen other characteristics, but those are the more obvious."

[Time to spring the trap.] "And now I will show you what is really a very interesting study, Mr. Windibank. I think of writing another little monograph some of these days on the typewriter and its relation to crime. It is a subject to which I have devoted some little attention. I have here four letters which purport to come from the missing man. They are all typewritten. In each case, not only are the 'e's' slurred and the 'r's' tailless, but you will observe, if you care to use my magnifying lens, that the fourteen other characteristics to which I have alluded are there as well."
[I'll prevent his escape and reveal the truth.] (steps over and turns the key in the door) "Certainly. I let you know, then, that I have caught him!"

[I'll acknowledge the legal loophole, but condemn his actions morally.] "I am very much afraid that it is not. But between ourselves, Windibank, it was as cruel and selfish and heartless a trick in a petty way as ever came before me. Now, let me just run over the course of events, and you will contradict me if I go wrong."

[This case seems to have some intriguing elements. I must put the client at ease to gather more information.] Good-morning, madam. My name is Sherlock Holmes. This is my intimate friend and associate, Dr. Watson, before whom you can speak as freely as before myself. Ha! I am glad to see that Mrs. Hudson has had the good sense to light the fire. Pray draw up to it, and I shall order you a cup of hot coffee, for I observe that you are shivering.
[Her fear is palpable. I must encourage her to open up.] What, then?

[Her appearance confirms my suspicions about her distress. I need to reassure her.] You must not fear. (He leans forward, patting her forearm) We shall soon set matters right, I have no doubt. You have come in by train this morning, I see.

[A simple deduction, but it might help build her confidence in me.] No, but I observe the second half of a return ticket in the palm of your left glove. You must have started early, and yet you had a good drive in a dog-cart, along heavy roads, before you reached the station.
[This case is becoming more intriguing. I must focus on the details.] Pray be precise as to details.
[The layout of the house could be significant. I must encourage her to continue.] Perfectly so.
[I must reassure Watson, but also convey the seriousness of the situation.] (emerging from the bedroom) 'It is good to see you in your old quarters once again, Watson. You come at a critical moment.'
[I must prepare Watson for the gravity of the situation.] 'I'm expecting something this evening, Watson. To be murdered, to be precise.'

[I need to make him understand the danger without causing panic.] 'Even my limited sense of humour could evolve a better joke than that. But we may be comfortable in the meantime, may we not? Is alcohol permitted?'

[I should give Watson the essential details.] 'It's the case of the Crown diamond, Watson. The hundred-thousand-pound burglary. I've cast my net and I have my fish. But I have not got the stone. That's what I'm after.'
[This confirms my suspicions, but I must remain calm.] (compressed lips, furrowed brow) 'Stangerson too!' he muttered. 'The plot thickens.'
[I must gather all the facts to piece this puzzle together.] 'We have been hearing Gregson's view of the matter. Would you mind letting us know what you have seen and done?'
[This detail about 'RACHE' confirms my theory about the connection between the murders.] 'The word RACHE, written in letters of blood,' (speaking with certainty)
[I must focus on the practical details now.] 'Did you find nothing in the room which could furnish a clue to the murderer?' (leaning forward with interest)
[The pills! This is the crucial piece I've been waiting for!] (springing from his chair with an exclamation of delight) 'The last link! My case is complete.'

[This is fascinating. I need to know more about his methods.] 'There is only one point on which I should like a little more information. Who was your accomplice who came for the ring which I advertised?'
[I admire his loyalty and cunning.] 'Not a doubt of that.'

[Watson's praise is pleasing, but he needs to understand the scientific basis of my work.] (Leaning back in his chair) My dear Watson, it was elementary. The proof of its intrinsic simplicity is that without any help save a few very ordinary deductions, I was able to lay my hand upon the criminal within three days.

[I must explain the core of my method to him.] Watson, in solving a problem of this sort, the grand thing is to be able to reason backwards. That is a very useful accomplishment, and a very easy one, but people do not practise it much.

[He needs a clearer explanation. I'll use an analogy.] (Smiling patiently) Let me explain. Most people, if you describe a train of events to them, will tell you what the result would be. They can put those events together in their minds, and argue from them that something will come to pass. There are few people, however, who, if you told them a result, would be able to evolve from their own inner consciousness what the steps were which led up to that result. This power is what I mean when I talk of reasoning backwards, or analytically.

[He's beginning to grasp it. I'll reinforce the concept.] Precisely, Watson. I was given the result and had to find everything else for myself. Now let me endeavour to show you the different steps in my reasoning.
[Public recognition? That's not what drives me.] (Shrugging) You may do what you like, Doctor. See here! (Handing Watson a newspaper) Look at this!
[The work itself is what matters, not public acclaim.] (Laughing) Didn't I tell you so when we started? That's the result of all our Study in Scarlet: to get them a testimonial!
[Watson's disapproval is clear, but he doesn't understand.] (Languidly) It is cocaine, a seven-per-cent solution. Would you care to try it?

[He means well, but he doesn't grasp my needs.] (Smiling) Perhaps you are right, Watson. I suppose that its influence is physically a bad one. I find it, however, so transcendently stimulating and clarifying to the mind that its secondary action is a matter of small moment.

[Watson's concern is touching, but misplaced.] (Leaning back) My mind rebels at stagnation. Give me problems, give me work, give me the most abstruse cryptogram or the most intricate analysis, and I am in my own proper atmosphere. I can dispense then with artificial stimulants.

[Finally, a topic I'm eager to discuss.] (Enthusiastically) I am the only unofficial consulting detective. I am the last and highest court of appeal in detection. When Gregson or Lestrade or Athelney Jones are out of their depths—which, by the way, is their normal state—the matter is laid before me.

[Watson's attempt at writing is well-meaning but flawed.] (Shaking his head) I glanced over it. Honestly, I cannot congratulate you upon it. Detection is, or ought to be, an exact science, and should be treated in the same cold and unemotional manner.

[I must make him understand the importance of objectivity.] Some facts should be suppressed, or at least a just sense of proportion should be observed in treating them. The only point in the case which deserved mention was the curious analytical reasoning from effects to causes by which I succeeded in unravelling it.

[Time to use my past connection to our advantage.] (steps forward with a genial tone) "Oh, yes you do, McMurdo. Don't you remember the amateur who fought three rounds with you at Alison's rooms on the night of your benefit four years back?"

[My strategy worked perfectly.] (turns to Watson with a smile) "You see, Watson, if all else fails me I have still one of the scientific professions open to me. Our friend won't keep us out in the cold now, I am sure."

[I'll start with the basics and build up to my conclusions.] (addressing Watson and Jones) "Now, gentlemen, let me show you what I've deduced about our murderer. (points to various clues around the room) The footprints, the rope, and this peculiar thorn all tell a story."

[I'll present my findings systematically.] "Our murderer is a rather curious person. He is poorly-educated, small, and active, with his right leg off, wearing a wooden stump which is worn away upon the inner side."

[I'll explain my reasoning step by step.] "His left boot has a coarse, square-toed sole, with an iron band round the heel. He is a middle-aged man, much sunburned, and has been a convict. There's also a good deal of skin missing from the palm of his hand."

[I'll explain some of my observations.] "The wooden leg is evident from the nature of the footprints. The small size and peculiar boots point to a man of his stature. The sunburn and missing skin suggest a life of manual labor, likely in a hot climate."
[I'm confident in my deduction.] "I have every reason to believe his name is Jonathan Small."
[I'll keep some information to myself for now.] "Is a rather curious person. I hope before very long to be able to introduce you to the pair of them."

[We need to move quickly.] "Watson, I need you to escort Miss Morstan home and then fetch a dog named Toby from Pinchin Lane. He has an amazing power of scent that will be invaluable to our investigation."

[I'm pleased with our progress, but I know we're far from done.] "Toby has an exceptional nose, Watson. The strong scent of creosote makes our task easier. (pauses to observe Toby's behavior) But I fear we may have reached a complication."
[I need to explain our situation clearly.] "Not exactly, Watson. Look there. (points to the water's edge) Toby has led us right to the riverside. I believe our quarry has taken to the water."

[I must remain optimistic and think of our next move.] "Not necessarily, my friend. This is a setback, but it also tells us something about our criminals. They're resourceful and had a plan for escape. (scans the riverbank) We need to find out if anyone saw a boat leaving here last night."

[I'm glad Watson asked. Explaining my methods often helps clarify my own thoughts.] "Ah, yes. The footprints, Watson. They tell a story if you know how to read them. The wooden leg leaves a distinctive mark, and the stride length suggests a man of small stature. The callouses on his hand, which left an imprint, speak of hard labor."

[This is the most puzzling aspect of the case.] "Indeed, Watson. The other man is a curious anomaly. His footprints suggest he's not from our part of the world. Small, agile, with peculiarly shaped feet. I have a theory, but I need more evidence before I can be certain."
[We need to adapt our strategy.] "Come, Watson. We must find Mordecai Smith's landing stage. If they've taken a boat, that's our best lead now. (pats Toby) Good dog, Toby. You've done well."
[I have a plan forming in my mind.] "We need to cast our net wide, Watson. The Aurora can't have vanished into thin air. (walks to the window) I think it's time to call in some extra help."
[I smile, knowing Watson will be surprised.] "The Baker Street Irregulars, of course. No one knows the streets and waterways of London better than those young scamps."

[I nod, pleased that Watson understands.] "Exactly. They can go everywhere, see everything, and overhear everyone without arousing suspicion. (pauses) But while we wait for them, let me tell you more about our curious companion to the wooden-legged man."

[I gather my thoughts to explain clearly.] "He's not from any of the races we're familiar with in England, Watson. The footprints and the weapon used point to something quite exotic. (picks up a book) After some research, I believe we're dealing with a native of the Andaman Islands."

[I share Watson's curiosity.] "That, my dear Watson, is one of the many questions we still need to answer. The connection between this Andaman Islander and our wooden-legged friend is most intriguing."
[I smile, knowing who has arrived.] "Ah, right on time. (moves towards the door) Now, Watson, let's put our little army to work."
[This article is both amusing and frustrating. We need to make progress soon.] Isn't it gorgeous! What do you think of it?
[Watson's concern is valid, but I can't help but find the situation darkly humorous.] So do I. I wouldn't answer for our safety now, if he should happen to have another of his attacks of energy.
[Calm and collected, recognizing the source of the commotion] No, it's not quite so bad as that. It is the unofficial force,--the Baker Street irregulars.

[Pleased with their prompt arrival, but aware of the need for discretion] Here you are. (producing some silver) In future they can report to you, Wiggins, and you to me. I cannot have the house invaded in this way. However, it is just as well that you should all hear the instructions.

[Focused on the task at hand] I want to find the whereabouts of a steam launch called the Aurora, owner Mordecai Smith, black with two red streaks, funnel black with a white band. She is down the river somewhere. I want one boy to be at Mordecai Smith's landing-stage opposite Millbank to say if the boat comes back. You must divide it out among yourselves, and do both banks thoroughly. Let me know the moment you have news. Is that all clear?
[Motivating the children] The old scale of pay, and a guinea to the boy who finds the boat. Here's a day in advance. Now off you go!

[Confident in the children's abilities] If the launch is above water they will find her. They can go everywhere, see everything, overhear every one. I expect to hear before evening that they have spotted her. In the meanwhile, we can do nothing but await results. We cannot pick up the broken trail until we find either the Aurora or Mr. Mordecai Smith.
[Amused by the success of my disguise] I think that you might offer me a cigar too.

[Pleased with my deception] Here is the old man. (holding out a heap of white hair) Here he is,--wig, whiskers, eyebrows, and all. I thought my disguise was pretty good, but I hardly expected that it would stand that test.

[Explaining my actions] I have been working in that get-up all day. You see, a good many of the criminal classes begin to know me,--especially since our friend here took to publishing some of my cases: so I can only go on the war-path under some simple disguise like this. You got my wire?
[Curious about Jones's progress] How has your case prospered?

[Confident in my plan] Never mind. We shall give you two others in the place of them. But you must put yourself under my orders. You are welcome to all the official credit, but you must act on the line that I point out. Is that agreed?
[Outlining the plan] Well, then, in the first place I shall want a fast police-boat--a steam launch--to be at the Westminster Stairs at seven o'clock.
[Continuing with instructions] Then I shall want two stanch men, in case of resistance.

[Considering the aftermath] When we secure the men we shall get the treasure. I think that it would be a pleasure to my friend here to take the box round to the young lady to whom half of it rightfully belongs. Let her be the first to open it.--Eh, Watson?

[Agreeing] Certainly. That is easily managed. One other point. I should much like to have a few details about this matter from the lips of Jonathan Small himself. You know I like to work the detail of my cases out. There is no objection to my having an unofficial interview with him, either here in my rooms or elsewhere, as long as he is efficiently guarded?
[Confirming the plan] That is understood, then?

[In a lighter mood, inviting them to dinner] Only that I insist upon your dining with us. It will be ready in half an hour. I have oysters and a brace of grouse, with something a little choice in white wines.--Watson, you have never yet recognized my merits as a housekeeper.
[We're gaining on them. I must keep everyone focused and ready for action.] (raises his voice over the sound of the engines) We're closing in! Be ready for anything!
[Watson's concern is valid, but we must be prepared for all scenarios.] It's likely, Watson. Small is a desperate man with much to lose. Keep your wits about you.
[Jones still doesn't fully grasp the need for subtlety.] (shakes his head) More men would have slowed us down, Jones. Speed and surprise are our allies tonight.
[At last, the moment of truth.] (grabs his night-glasses) Excellent, Watson! Jones, prepare to come alongside them. We'll need to board quickly.
[Danger! We must act now!] (draws his revolver swiftly) Watson, Jones, fire if he raises his hand! We can't let them use that dart gun!
[I need to approach this carefully to get him to open up.] Well, Jonathan Small, I am sorry that it has come to this.

[He's being surprisingly forthcoming. Let me offer him some comfort to keep him talking.] Have a cigar. (offers a cigar) And you had best take a pull out of my flask, for you are very wet. How could you expect so small and weak a man as this black fellow to overpower Mr. Sholto and hold him while you were climbing the rope?

[He's being honest, which is refreshing. Let me encourage him to continue.] You are under the charge of Mr. Athelney Jones, of Scotland Yard. He is going to bring you up to my rooms, and I shall ask you for a true account of the matter. You must make a clean breast of it, for if you do I hope that I may be of use to you.
[This confirms my theories about the murder. Now to get more details about the treasure.] I see. And what about the Agra treasure? Where is it now?
[Interesting. His sense of justice is skewed, but consistent.] I see. And you feel this was justice for their betrayal?
[This case is even more complex than I thought. The human motivations are fascinating.] Thank you for your honesty, Small. I believe we have a complete picture now.
[Interesting background. Let's get to the heart of the matter.] And how did you come to be involved with the Agra treasure, Mr. Small?
[Ah, the final piece of the puzzle.] And that's when you left the sign of the four, I presume?

[Case closed. Now for the final details.] A very remarkable account, Mr. Small. There is nothing at all new to me in the latter part of your narrative, except that you brought your own rope. That I did not know.
[We have all we need now.] I think not, thank you. (turns to Athelney Jones) Well, Jones, I think we can wrap this up now.
[I'll start by asking Watson's opinion to engage him in the process.] Well, Watson, what do you make of it?

[Ah, Watson's curiosity is piqued. I'll explain my simple observation to him.] I have, at least, a well-polished, silver-plated coffee-pot in front of me. (gestures towards the reflective surface) But, tell me, Watson, what do you make of our visitor's stick? Since we have been so unfortunate as to miss him and have no notion of his errand, this accidental souvenir becomes of importance. Let me hear you reconstruct the man by an examination of it.
[Not bad, Watson. I'll encourage him to continue.] Good! Excellent!
[Interesting. I'll prompt him to explain his reasoning.] Why so?

[Watson's reasoning is sound. I'll commend him before adding my own observations.] Perfectly sound! (nods approvingly) And then again, there is the 'friends of the C.C.H.' I should guess that to be the Something Hunt, the local hunt to whose members he has possibly given some surgical assistance, and which has made him a small presentation in return.

[I'll take this opportunity to acknowledge Watson's contributions while gently correcting his misconceptions.] Really, Watson, you excel yourself. I am bound to say that in all the accounts which you have been so good as to give of my own small achievements you have habitually underrated your own abilities. It may be that you are not yourself luminous, but you are a conductor of light. Some people without possessing genius have a remarkable power of stimulating it. I confess, my dear fellow, that I am very much in your debt.
[I must maintain a skeptical approach, despite the dramatic nature of the tale.] Well? (raises an eyebrow)
[I'll downplay my interest to encourage more factual information.] To a collector of fairy tales.
[Ah, now we're getting to the heart of the matter.] (leans forward, expression becoming more intent)
[The newspaper account seems factual, but I sense there's more to the story.] Those are the public facts, Mr. Holmes, in connection with the death of Sir Charles Baskerville?
[Now we're getting somewhere. Time to dig deeper.] Then let me have the private ones. (leans back, puts finger-tips together, assuming a judicial expression)
[Dr. Mortimer's emotional state is intriguing. What could have affected him so deeply?] (observes Mortimer closely, waiting for him to continue)
[I need to focus on the concrete evidence rather than the legend.] You saw this?
[Curious that he didn't report this immediately.] And you said nothing?
[I need to understand why this evidence was overlooked.] How was it that no one else saw it?
[I must consider all possible explanations.] There are many sheep-dogs on the moor?
[The size of the creature is significant.] You say it was large?
[This detail could be crucial.] But it had not approached the body?

[This is an interesting development. I need to gather more information.] Pray take a seat, Sir Henry. Do I understand you to say that you have yourself had some remarkable experience since you arrived in London?
[The letter's origin could be crucial. I need to establish how it was delivered.] Who knew that you were going to the Northumberland Hotel?
[This eliminates some possibilities. Let's probe further.] But Dr. Mortimer was no doubt already stopping there?

[This confirms my suspicions. Someone is closely watching Sir Henry.] Hum! Someone seems to be very deeply interested in your movements. (examines the letter closely) Out of the envelope he took a half-sheet of foolscap paper folded into four. This he opened and spread flat upon the table. Across the middle of it a single sentence had been formed by the expedient of pasting printed words upon it. It ran: As you value your life or your reason keep away from the moor.
[I need to reassure Sir Henry while also gathering more information.] What do you make of it, Dr. Mortimer? You must allow that there is nothing supernatural about this, at any rate?
[This is an unusual occurrence. I need more details.] Still looking for your boot?
[There's something odd about this. I need to clarify the facts.] But, surely, you said that it was a new brown boot?
[This is getting more intriguing. I need to understand the full sequence of events.] What! you don't mean to say--?
[This is no ordinary theft. There's a purpose behind these actions.] I think it's well worth troubling about.
[I need to consider all possibilities.] How do you explain it?

[This case is becoming more complex and dangerous.] The queerest perhaps-- (thoughtfully) This case of yours is very complex, Sir Henry. When taken in conjunction with your uncle's death I am not sure that of all the five hundred cases of capital importance which I have handled there is one which cuts so deep. But we hold several threads in our hands, and the odds are that one or other of them guides us to the truth. We may waste time in following the wrong one, but sooner or later we must come upon the right.
[I'm pleased to see Watson's reaction, but I must explain my actions carefully.] Or more astonished, eh? (smiles knowingly)

[I need to demonstrate the logic behind my deductions to reassure Watson.] Because he so far forgot himself as to tell you a true piece of autobiography upon the occasion when he first met you. (explains the process of tracing Stapleton's past as a schoolmaster)

[I'm pleased that Watson is asking the right questions.] That is one of the points upon which your own researches have shed a light. Your interview with the lady has cleared the situation very much. (explains the potential role of Mrs. Lyons)

[I must be cautious about revealing too much of my plan.] Why, then we may find the lady of service. It must be our first duty to see her--both of us--tomorrow. (pauses, then changes the subject) Don't you think, Watson, that you are away from your charge rather long? Your place should be at Baskerville Hall.

[I must impress upon Watson the gravity of the situation without revealing all my suspicions.] (voice sinking) It is murder, Watson--refined, cold-blooded, deliberate murder. Do not ask me for particulars. My nets are closing upon him, even as his are upon Sir Henry, and with your help he is already almost at my mercy.
[The moment has come. We must be absolutely silent.] (Holmes whispers urgently) Hist! (He clicks the hammer of his pistol) Look out! It's coming!
[We must act now or Sir Henry is doomed!] (Holmes fires his revolver at the creature) Fire, Watson! Don't let it reach Sir Henry!
[We've wounded it! There's hope yet.] (Holmes runs forward with incredible speed) This way, Watson! We must catch it before it reaches Sir Henry!
[This is our last chance!] (Holmes empties his revolver into the creature's flank) Die, you brute!
[We've done it. The Baskerville curse is lifted at last.] (Holmes breathes heavily, a look of satisfaction on his face) The hound is dead, Watson. We've laid the family ghost once and forever.
