[We've made significant progress, but I must keep Watson focused.] We're at close grips at last, Watson. (Holmes speaks confidently as they walk) What a nerve the fellow has! How he pulled himself together in the face of what must have been a paralyzing shock when he found that the wrong man had fallen a victim to his plot. I told you in London, Watson, and I tell you now again, that we have never had a foeman more worthy of our steel.
[Watson's concern is touching, but unnecessary.] And so was I at first. But there was no getting out of it.

[I must consider all possibilities.] It may cause him to be more cautious, or it may drive him to desperate measures at once. Like most clever criminals, he may be too confident in his own cleverness and imagine that he has completely deceived us.

[Watson's eagerness is admirable, but premature.] (Holmes smiles slightly) My dear Watson, you were born to be a man of action. Your instinct is always to do something energetic. But supposing, for argument's sake, that we had him arrested tonight, what on earth the better off should we be for that? We could prove nothing against him. There's the devilish cunning of it! If he were acting through a human agent we could get some evidence, but if we were to drag this great dog to the light of day it would not help us in putting a rope round the neck of its master.
[I must make Watson understand the complexity of the situation.] Not a shadow of one--only surmise and conjecture. We should be laughed out of court if we came with such a story and such evidence.

[Watson's persistence is admirable, but I must explain the legal challenges.] Found dead without a mark upon him. You and I know that he died of sheer fright, and we know also what frightened him, but how are we to get twelve stolid jurymen to know it? What signs are there of a hound? Where are the marks of its fangs? Of course we know that a hound does not bite a dead body and that Sir Charles was dead before ever the brute overtook him. But we have to prove all this, and we are not in a position to do it.

[I shall begin with Stapleton's background, as it's crucial to understanding his motives.] The whole course of events, from the point of view of the man who called himself Stapleton was simple and direct, although to us, who had no means in the beginning of knowing the motives of his actions and could only learn part of the facts, it all appeared exceedingly complex.

[I must organize my thoughts to present a clear narrative.] Certainly, though I cannot guarantee that I carry all the facts in my mind. Intense mental concentration has a curious way of blotting out what has passed. (Holmes pauses, collecting his thoughts) My inquiries show beyond all question that the family portrait did not lie, and that this fellow was indeed a Baskerville. He was a son of that Rodger Baskerville, the younger brother of Sir Charles, who fled with a sinister reputation to South America, where he was said to have died unmarried.

[I must explain Stapleton's journey to England and his motivations.] Indeed. He married Beryl Garcia in Costa Rica, then changed his name to Vandeleur and fled to England after embezzling public funds. He established a school in Yorkshire, which eventually fell into disrepute. The Vandeleurs then changed their name to Stapleton, and he brought his remaining fortune, future schemes, and passion for entomology to the south of England.

[Now I must explain the core of Stapleton's plot.] When he went to Devonshire, his plans were initially hazy, but he clearly meant mischief from the start. He took his wife with him under the guise of being his sister, intending to use her as a decoy. His ultimate goal was to claim the Baskerville estate, and he was prepared to use any means necessary to achieve this end.

[I must detail Stapleton's ingenious yet horrific plan.] Stapleton learned of the family legend of the hound from Sir Charles himself. Knowing the old man's weak heart and superstitious nature, he devised a plan to use these against him. He acquired a large savage hound from London and made it appear demonic using phosphorus paint. (Holmes leans forward, his voice lowering) The use of artificial means to make the creature diabolical was a flash of genius on his part, Watson.

[Now I must explain the role of Mrs. Lyons.] Stapleton manipulated Mrs. Laura Lyons into writing a letter to Sir Charles, requesting a late-night meeting. He then prevented her from attending, ensuring Sir Charles would be alone when he unleashed the hound. The poor man fled in terror, succumbing to heart failure at the end of the Yew Alley.

[I shall explain my methods and the final confrontation.] Ah, Watson, that's where the game became truly interesting. (Holmes smiles, a glint in his eye) I had my suspicions from the start, particularly after detecting the scent of white jessamine on the anonymous note. As for Sir Henry, Stapleton attempted to use the same method, but we were there to thwart him. In the end, it was his wife's rebellion against his schemes that proved his undoing.
[This cipher looks intriguing. I must approach it methodically.] Watson, this message is clearly an attempt to convey secret information. We need to determine which book it refers to.

[Watson's suggestion is logical, but not quite right.] Good, Watson, good! But not, if I may say so, quite good enough. The Bible has too many editions with different paginations. We need a standardized book.
[Watson is getting closer, but still not quite there.] There are difficulties, Watson. The vocabulary of Bradshaw is nervous and terse, but limited. We need something else.
[Excellent deduction from Watson!] (smiles) Excellent, Watson! I am very much mistaken if you have not touched the spot. An almanac! Let us consider the claims of Whitaker's Almanac.

[This message is more significant than I initially thought.] (looks intently at Watson) There, Watson! What do you think of pure reason and its fruit? 'There is danger--may--come--very soon--one. Douglas--rich--country--now--at Birlstone--House--Birlstone--confidence--is--pressing.'

[This confirms the warning in the message. The game is afoot!] (raises an eyebrow) Remarkable! I'm interested, Mr. Mac, but hardly surprised. It seems our anonymous friend's warning was timely, if not entirely effective.

[I must explain the situation to MacDonald.] (calmly) You see, Inspector, we received an anonymous communication warning of danger to a certain person. Within an hour, we learn that this danger has materialized. It's a matter of interest, certainly, but not surprise.

[I must emphasize the importance of Moriarty's role in the criminal world.] Inspector, you must understand that Professor Moriarty is no ordinary criminal. He is the Napoleon of crime, the organizer of half that is evil and nearly all that is undetected in this great city.

[MacDonald's skepticism is understandable, but dangerous.] (smiles wryly) I'm glad you've got so far as to recognize the talent, Inspector. But respectability is merely a facade. Let me give you some details about Moriarty's operation.

[I must provide concrete examples to convince MacDonald.] Did you know, Inspector, that Moriarty pays his chief of staff, Colonel Sebastian Moran, six thousand a year? That's more than the Prime Minister gets. And his wealth is spread across at least six different banks, possibly more.

[Now to link this to the current case.] There could be two motives for the murder, Inspector. Either Douglas betrayed Moriarty and was punished, or Moriarty engineered the crime as part of his regular business. In either case, the answers lie in Birlstone.
[The game is afoot. We must move quickly.] (nods to Watson) Indeed, Watson. We'll need to leave immediately. Inspector, what details do you have about the Birlstone case?
[Intriguing. This case promises to be stimulating.] (eyes gleaming) Excellent. And what of the victim, John Douglas?
[We have a starting point, but much remains to be discovered.] (stands up, ready to leave) Then we have our work cut out for us, gentlemen. To Birlstone, and let us see what secrets this case holds.
[Interesting choice of weapon. That could be significant.] (leans forward, eyes gleaming with interest) Indeed, a most peculiar choice. Please continue, Mr. Mason.
[Ah, a clue!] A big P with a flourish above it, E and N smaller?
[It's essential to maintain focus on the case rather than my methods.] (waves dismissively) Pennsylvania Small Arms Company – a well-known American firm. But pray, continue with the other details.
[Both have valid points. I need more data.] (steeples fingers) Gentlemen, you both raise interesting points. Mr. Mason, what about the moat? Was it examined for signs of someone crossing?
[We need to see the scene firsthand.] (stands up) I believe it's time we visited the house. Seeing the layout and evidence in person will be invaluable.
[There's a potential connection here.] (leans forward, eyes narrowing) Mr. Barker, did you know Mrs. Douglas before the marriage?
[His reaction is telling.] (observing Barker closely) Did Mr. Douglas entirely approve of your friendship with his wife?

[There's something odd about the lighting.] (thoughtfully) You mentioned earlier that when you entered the room, only a candle was lit on the table. Yet when help arrived, the lamp was on and the candle out. Can you explain that?
[I need to start with the most glaring inconsistency.] Watson, what strikes you as the most peculiar aspect of this case?
[Ah, a good starting point, but not the crux of the matter.] Indeed, their behavior is curious, but let's focus on the crime scene itself. What about the timeline of events?

[I need to guide him to see the inconsistency.] Consider this, Watson. How long would it take for an assassin to remove the wedding ring, replace another ring, and place that curious card beside the body?

[Now to drive the point home.] Exactly. And yet, according to the official story, the assassin had less than a minute after the murder before Barker and Mrs. Douglas arrived. It's simply not possible.
[He's grasping it now.] Precisely, Watson. And if that's the case, what does it tell us about Barker and Mrs. Douglas?
[Now to introduce the conspiracy theory.] Not just lying, Watson. I believe they're in a conspiracy to conceal something. The question is, what are they hiding and why?

[A valid point that needs addressing.] An excellent question, Watson. That's why I don't believe they're necessarily the murderers. They might be protecting someone else, or concealing some other secret entirely.

[Time to mention my plans for further investigation.] Not yet, my dear Watson, but I intend to spend an evening alone in that study. I believe the atmosphere of the room might provide the inspiration I need to unravel this mystery.
[This is interesting, but I'm not entirely convinced.] Excellent work, gentlemen. Please, tell me more about this Hargrave.
[The description is intriguing.] Interesting. That could almost be a description of Douglas himself, barring the expression. What else do we know?
[I'm considering how this fits with my theories.] It's certainly a promising lead. But I'm curious, why would he leave his bicycle behind if he needed to make a quick escape?
[I need to propose an alternative theory.] Consider this, gentlemen. What if Hargrave is indeed our killer, but he's not working alone? What if someone inside the house is helping him?

[I need to be careful not to accuse without evidence.] I'm not accusing anyone, Inspector. I'm merely pointing out that we need to consider all possibilities. The behavior of those in the house is as crucial to this case as the actions of our mysterious American.

[It's time to propose my theory about a deeper conspiracy.] Those details, Mr. Mason, are precisely why I believe there's more to this story. They suggest a personal vendetta, possibly dating back to Douglas's past in America.

[I need to explain my next steps.] I intend to spend an evening alone in the study where the murder took place. I believe the atmosphere of the room might provide the inspiration I need to unravel this mystery.
[I must set the stage for Douglas's explanation.] Gentlemen, as you can see, Mr. John Douglas is very much alive. I believe he has quite a tale to tell us.
[I'm keenly interested in the details.] Please, Mr. Douglas, tell us about these men and why they were after you.
[I'm impressed by the ingenuity, but concerned about the implications.] A clever plan, Mr. Douglas. But I fear it may not be enough to ensure your safety in the long run.
[I must warn him of the danger.] I fear your enemies are not so easily fooled. They may suspect a ruse, especially now that the case has gained such publicity. You may still be in grave danger.

[I consider the gravity of the situation.] For now, Mr. Douglas, I suggest you remain in hiding. I'll need to think carefully about how to ensure your long-term safety. This case may be solved, but I fear your troubles are far from over.
[I suspected this might happen. I must remain calm and gather more information.] I feared as much. (He maintains a composed demeanor) You have not had a cable, have you?

[Just as I thought. Now to confirm the details.] It's poor Douglas. They tell me his name is Edwards; but he will always be Jack Douglas of Benito Canyon to me. I told you that they started together for South Africa in the Palmyra three weeks ago.
[Now for the crucial information.] The ship reached Cape Town last night. I received this cable from Mrs. Douglas this morning:
'Jack has been lost overboard in gale off St. Helena. No one knows how accident occurred.' 'IVY DOUGLAS.'
[This confirms my suspicions. It's too neat, too convenient.] (His eyes narrowing in thought) Well, I've no doubt it was well stage-managed.
[I must be careful how much I reveal. Barker isn't ready for the full truth.] None in the world.
[He's catching on, but he doesn't see the bigger picture yet.] Surely!

[I need to redirect his thinking. This goes beyond the Scowrers.] (Interrupting firmly) No, no, my good sir. There is a master hand here. It is no case of sawed-off shotguns and clumsy six-shooters. You can tell an old master by the sweep of his brush. I can tell a Moriarty when I see one. This crime is from London, not from America.

[Interesting. He's trying to maintain his authority, but he's clearly uncomfortable.] Pray take a seat. This is my friend and colleague, Dr. Watson, who is occasionally good enough to help me in my cases. Whom have I the honour to address?
[Watson's presence could be valuable. I won't let him leave.] It is both, or none. You may say before this gentleman anything which you may say to me.
[This case is even more significant than I initially thought.] I promise.

[Just as I suspected. His mannerisms and the quality of his attire gave it away.] Why, indeed? Your Majesty had not spoken before I was aware that I was addressing Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein, Grand Duke of Cassel-Felstein, and hereditary King of Bohemia.
[Now we're getting to the heart of the matter.] Then, pray consult.
[Ah, Irene Adler. This case just became even more interesting.] (Without opening his eyes) Kindly look her up in my index, Doctor.

[Let's see what we know about Ms. Adler.] Let me see! Born in New Jersey in the year 1858. Contralto--hum! La Scala, hum! Prima donna Imperial Opera of Warsaw--yes! Retired from operatic stage--ha! Living in London--quite so! Your Majesty, as I understand, became entangled with this young person, wrote her some compromising letters, and is now desirous of getting those letters back.
[This case promises to be most interesting.] Mr. Wilson, pray tell us from the beginning about your experience with this Red-Headed League.
[Curious indeed. The specificity of the hair color requirement is most unusual.] And you applied for this position, I presume?
[There must be more to this than simple copying work.] How long did this arrangement continue, Mr. Wilson?
[This case is proving to be most intriguing.] (Steepling his fingers) Mr. Wilson, have you noticed anything unusual about your assistant, Vincent Spaulding, since this incident?

[This case is shaping up to be quite the puzzle.] It may be, Watson. Mr. Wilson, I believe we have all the facts we need for now. I shall need to think on this matter. You may expect a resolution to your problem very soon.

[I'll start with a bold statement to capture Watson's attention.] "My dear fellow, life is infinitely stranger than anything which the mind of man could invent. We would not dare to conceive the things which are really mere commonplaces of existence."

[Watson's skepticism is understandable, but I must explain the nuances he's missing.] "A certain selection and discretion must be used in producing a realistic effect. This is wanting in the police report, where more stress is laid, perhaps, upon the platitudes of the magistrate than upon the details, which to an observer contain the vital essence of the whole matter. Depend upon it, there is nothing so unnatural as the commonplace."

[Ah, the perfect opportunity to prove my point. I'll use this very example to demonstrate the unexpected nature of real cases.] "Indeed, your example is an unfortunate one for your argument. (takes the paper and glances his eye down it) This is the Dundas separation case, and, as it happens, I was engaged in clearing up some small points in connection with it. The husband was a teetotaler, there was no other woman, and the conduct complained of was that he had drifted into the habit of winding up every meal by taking out his false teeth and hurling them at his wife, which, you will allow, is not an action likely to occur to the imagination of the average story-teller. Take a pinch of snuff, Doctor, and acknowledge that I have scored over you in your example."

[Watson's observation gives me an opportunity to further illustrate the fascinating nature of my work.] "Ah, I forgot that I had not seen you for some weeks. It is a little souvenir from the King of Bohemia in return for my assistance in the case of the Irene Adler papers."

[I'm pleased by Watson's interest, though I must maintain some discretion.] "It was from the reigning family of Holland, though the matter in which I served them was of such delicacy that I cannot confide it even to you, who have been good enough to chronicle one or two of my little problems."

[I appreciate Watson's interest, but I must admit that my current cases lack the excitement of previous ones.] "Some ten or twelve, but none which present any feature of interest. They are important, you understand, without being interesting. Indeed, I have found that it is usually in unimportant matters that there is a field for the observation, and for the quick analysis of cause and effect which gives the charm to an investigation."
[This young man is clearly distressed. Let me put him at ease.] Give me your coat and umbrella. They may rest here on the hook and will be dry presently. You have come up from the south-west, I see.

[A simple deduction, but it always impresses clients.] That clay and chalk mixture which I see upon your toe caps is quite distinctive. (gestures to a chair) Please, sit down and tell me why you've come.
[Ah, the Tankerville Club case. A simple matter, really.] He said that you could solve anything, did he not?
[I must temper his expectations, but also show confidence.] I have been beaten four times--three times by men, and once by a woman. But what is that compared with the number of my successes?
[Now to get to the heart of the matter.] I beg that you will draw your chair up to the fire and favour me with some details as to your case.

[This promises to be most interesting indeed.] You fill me with interest. Pray give us the essential facts from the commencement, and I can afterwards question you as to those details which seem to me to be most important.
[I feared as much. This is a grave failure on my part.] (voice calm but strained) Ah! I feared as much. How was it done?

[This is my fault. I should have acted more quickly.] (clenches fists) That hurts my pride, Watson. It becomes a personal matter with me now, and, if God sends me health, I shall set my hand upon this gang.

[I should have anticipated their swift action. I won't make that mistake again.] They must be cunning devils. How could they have decoyed him down there? The Embankment is not on the direct line to the station.
[I will not rest until I've solved this case.] I shall be my own police. When I have spun the web they may take the flies, but not before.
[I appreciate Watson's offer, but this is something I must do alone.] Not at present, Watson. I shall be busy for the next day or so. When I've finished, we'll discuss it fully.

[I must maintain my disguise while explaining to Watson.] (in a low voice) As low as you can. I have excellent ears. If you would have the great kindness to get rid of that sottish friend of yours I should be exceedingly glad to have a little talk with you.

[Good, we can speak more freely once Isa is gone.] Then pray send him home in it. You may safely trust him, for he appears to be too limp to get into any mischief. I should recommend you also to send a note by the cabman to your wife to say that you have thrown in your lot with me.
[We must move quickly but cautiously.] If you will wait outside, I shall be with you in five minutes.

[Now to explain the situation to Watson.] (stretching) I suppose, Watson, that you imagine that I have added opium-smoking to cocaine injections, and all the other little weaknesses on which you have favoured me with your medical views.

[Time to reveal the true nature of my presence here.] I am in the midst of a very remarkable inquiry, and I have hoped to find a clue in the incoherent ramblings of these sots, as I have done before now.

[I need Watson's help on this one.] It's the disappearance of Mr. Neville St. Clair, a respectable businessman. His wife last saw him at the window of this very opium den. Watson, will you accompany me to their home in Lee, Kent? I could use your assistance.
[I must give St. Clair a chance to explain himself.] (gently) Mr. St. Clair, I believe it's time you shared your story with us. How did you come to lead this double life?
[His motivations are clear, but we need to address the events of his disappearance.] Mr. St. Clair, can you explain what happened on the day your wife saw you at the window?

[We must consider the family in this situation.] Inspector, while Mr. St. Clair's actions are certainly questionable, no actual crime has been committed. Perhaps we can resolve this matter discreetly?

[I'll start with the background of St. Clair.] Neville St. Clair, Watson, is a man of respectable standing who came to Lee in May 1884. He married a local brewer's daughter and has two children. He commutes to London daily for work.

[Now to the crux of the matter.] Last Monday, St. Clair went to London earlier than usual. His wife received a telegram and went to the city to collect a parcel. While there, she passed through Swandam Lane.
[Precisely.] Exactly. As Mrs. St. Clair walked down the lane, she heard a cry and saw her husband at a second-floor window of the opium den. He looked agitated and vanished suddenly from the window.

[Her actions were quite sensible.] She tried to enter the building but was stopped by a Lascar and his Danish assistant. Fortunately, she found a police inspector and two constables nearby. They searched the room where St. Clair had been seen.

[This is where it gets peculiar.] They found no trace of St. Clair. Instead, they encountered a hideous cripple named Hugh Boone, a professional beggar. St. Clair's clothes were discovered behind a curtain, but the man himself was gone.
[Indeed, but there's more.] They did arrest Boone, but the case took an unexpected turn. This morning, Mrs. St. Clair received a letter from her husband, posted yesterday.

[That's what we're going to find out.] The letter assured her that all would be well. It's this new development that we're heading to Lee to investigate. The game is afoot, Watson, and it's more complex than it first appeared.
[Let's start with the obvious.] Well, Watson, what can you make of this hat?
[Perfect opportunity to explain my methods.] On the contrary, Watson, you can see everything. You fail, however, to reason from what you see.

[I'll start with the intellectual capacity of the owner.] That the man is highly intellectual is obvious upon the face of it. (picks up the hat) This hat is of the very best quality. Look at the band of ribbed silk and the excellent lining.
[I'll demonstrate.] (puts the hat on his head) It is a question of cubic capacity, Watson. A man with so large a brain must have something in it.

[Now for the man's circumstances.] He is middle-aged, has grizzled hair which he has had cut within the last few days, and which he anoints with lime-cream. His wife has ceased to love him, he is out of training entirely, and he is middle-aged.

[I'll explain each deduction in turn.] The hair-ends are newly cut, and there's an odor of lime-cream. The dust on the hat shows it's been hung up indoors, indicating a sedentary lifestyle. As for his wife, when I see you with a week's accumulation of dust upon your hat, Watson, I shall fear that you have been unfortunate enough to lose your wife's affection.
[I have an answer for everything.] Nay, he was bringing home the goose as a peace-offering to his wife. Remember the card upon the bird's leg.

[I must remain perfectly still and alert. Any sound or movement could be crucial.] (whispers) Watson, do not go asleep; your very life may depend upon it. Have your pistol ready in case we should need it.
[This is it! The moment we've been waiting for.] (tenses, ready to spring into action)
[It's the snake! I must act now!] (leaps from the bed, strikes a match, and lashes furiously with his cane at the bell-pull) You see it, Watson? You see it?
[It's over. The snake has turned on its master.] It means that it is all over. And perhaps, after all, it is for the best. Take your pistol, and we will enter Dr. Roylott's room.

[Justice has been served, albeit in an unexpected manner.] The band! The speckled band! (approaches cautiously) It is a swamp adder, the deadliest snake in India. He has died within ten seconds of being bitten. Violence does, in truth, recoil upon the violent, and the schemer falls into the pit which he digs for another.

[This case seems quite straightforward, but I must maintain an air of mystery to keep the client engaged.] Good-day, Lord St. Simon. Pray take the basket-chair. This is my friend and colleague, Dr. Watson. Draw up a little to the fire, and we will talk this matter over.
[He's concerned about social standing. I'll put him at ease with a touch of intrigue.] No, I am descending.
[A little name-dropping should impress him.] My last client of the sort was a king.
[I must maintain client confidentiality, even with royalty.] The King of Scandinavia.
[Time to redirect the conversation to the matter at hand.] You can understand that I extend to the affairs of my other clients the same secrecy which I promise to you in yours.

[Now to begin the real investigation.] Thank you. I have already learned all that is in the public prints, nothing more. I presume that I may take it as correct--this article, for example, as to the disappearance of the bride.
[Time to dig deeper.] But it needs a great deal of supplementing before anyone could offer an opinion. I think that I may arrive at my facts most directly by questioning you.

[This case seems to involve a person of considerable standing. I must approach it with care.] I remember you well, Mr. Holder. Please, take a seat and tell me what brings you here today. From your demeanor, I can see it's a matter of great urgency.

[A national treasure involved? This case is even more significant than I initially thought.] I see. This is indeed a serious matter. Please, Mr. Holder, start from the beginning. Tell me every detail, no matter how insignificant it may seem to you.
[Taking such a valuable item home seems unwise. There must be more to this decision.] And you felt it was safer in your home than in the bank? That's an unusual choice for a banker.
[This personal responsibility might be key to understanding the events.] I understand. Now, tell me about the night of the theft. What exactly did you see and hear?
[This is a crucial moment in the narrative. I need more details about Arthur's behavior.] And how did your son react when you confronted him?
[There are several possibilities here. I need to consider all angles.] I see. Mr. Holder, before we go any further, I need to ask: do you receive much company at your home?
[This Sir George Burnwell might be worth looking into.] Every detail is potentially important, Mr. Holder. Now, tell me more about your household. Who else was present on the night of the theft?

[I must start from the beginning to help Mr. Holder understand the sequence of events.] Mr. Holder, let me explain what occurred in your house that night. Your niece, when she thought you had gone to your room, slipped down to speak with her lover through the window facing the stable lane.
[I must reveal the painful truth, but gently.] It was Sir George Burnwell, a man of evil reputation among women. Your niece told him about the coronet, and his greed was kindled by the news.
[I must help him understand Mary's motivations.] Mr. Holder, there are women in whom the love of a lover extinguishes all other loves. I believe your niece may have been one such woman.
[I must highlight Arthur's noble character.] Your son, Mr. Holder, acted with great chivalry. He discovered the truth but chose to protect his cousin, even at the cost of his own reputation.
[I should provide some closure regarding the coronet.] I managed to recover the stones, Mr. Holder. They cost me £3000, which was infinitely less than what you were willing to pay.
[I must be direct but compassionate.] I'm afraid she has fled with Sir George Burnwell. But rest assured, Mr. Holder, whatever her sins are, they will soon receive more than sufficient punishment.

[I need to address Watson's writing style directly.] Watson, I must say that in these little records of our cases, you have given prominence not so much to the many causes célèbres and sensational trials in which I have figured but rather to those incidents which may have been trivial in themselves, but which have given room for those faculties of deduction and of logical synthesis which I have made my special province.

[I must clarify my point without dismissing Watson's efforts entirely.] (lighting his pipe) You have erred, perhaps, in attempting to put colour and life into each of your statements instead of confining yourself to the task of placing upon record that severe reasoning from cause to effect which is really the only notable feature about the thing.

[I must explain my perspective more clearly.] No, it is not selfishness or conceit. If I claim full justice for my art, it is because it is an impersonal thing--a thing beyond myself. Crime is common. Logic is rare. Therefore it is upon the logic rather than upon the crime that you should dwell.

[I must emphasize the importance of logical analysis.] Pshaw, my dear fellow, what do the public, the great unobservant public, who could hardly tell a weaver by his tooth or a compositor by his left thumb, care about the finer shades of analysis and deduction!

[I should acknowledge the value of Watson's approach while reiterating my own.] The human element has its place, Watson, but it is the cold, hard logic that truly solves the case. That is what sets our work apart from mere sensationalism.

[I feel a mix of frustration and hope.] (sighing) To be honest, Watson, I fear my little practice is degenerating. But this note I had this morning might prove interesting. It's from a Miss Violet Hunter, seeking advice on whether to accept a position as a governess.
[I sense her urgency and need to reassure her.] Pray tell us what has happened to you.
[I need to ensure we get a clear, chronological account.] Let us have everything in its due order. (leans forward, fingers steepled)
[This is an intriguing start. I need more specifics.] What can you not understand?
[These details are significant. I must probe further.] And what of your duties? Were they as described in the advertisement?

[This pipe could be the key to understanding our impatient visitor. I must examine it closely.] (picks up the pipe and begins to examine it) Well, well, you did your best. It's very annoying, though, Watson. I was badly in need of a case, and this looks, from the man's impatience, as if it were of importance.

[The pipe's quality and the man's behavior are telling. I must share my observations with Watson.] (continuing to examine the pipe) Hullo! That's not your pipe on the table. He must have left his behind him. A nice old brier with a good long stem of what the tobacconists call amber.
[The rarity of genuine amber mouthpieces could be significant.] I wonder how many real amber mouthpieces there are in London? Some people think that a fly in it is a sign.
[The fact that the man left such a valuable item indicates his state of mind.] Well, he must have been disturbed in his mind to leave a pipe behind him which he evidently values highly.

[Watson's question gives me an opportunity to explain my reasoning.] Well, I should put the original cost of the pipe at seven and sixpence. Now it has, you see, been twice mended, once in the wooden stem and once in the amber. Each of these mends, done, as you observe, with silver bands, must have cost more than the pipe did originally. The man must value the pipe highly when he prefers to patch it up rather than buy a new one with the same money.

[There's always more to observe, if one knows how to look.] (examines the pipe more closely) Indeed, Watson. The pipe tells us that he is a left-handed man of nervous disposition, with a fair income but careless habits. These are just preliminary observations, of course. We shall see what else we can glean when our visitor returns.

[The emotional resolution of this case is now in their hands. We should give them privacy.] (turning to Watson) I believe our work here is done, Watson. Mr. Munro, Mrs. Munro, we'll take our leave now. I trust you both have much to discuss.
[His distress is evident. Time to press further.] I am an accountant.
[His behavior confirms my suspicions.] (whispering) What now? Is he giving us the slip?
[Something is terribly wrong!] (springing into action) We must break down this door immediately!
[I feel a sense of nostalgia as I recall this case.] Watson, let me tell you about my very first case. It all began during my college days when I met Victor Trevor.
[I remember the details vividly.] It was quite by accident. Trevor's bull terrier bit my ankle one morning as I was going to chapel. This led to our acquaintance and eventual friendship.
[I recall my youthful enthusiasm.] Indeed, Watson. Trevor invited me to his father's place in Norfolk for the long vacation. It was there that I first exercised my powers of deduction on Old Trevor.

[I remember the mixed results of my deductions.] I made some observations about his past - his boxing, his travels to New Zealand and Japan. But I also touched upon a sensitive subject that caused him to faint.

[I recall the gravity of the situation.] I mentioned that he had been intimately associated with someone whose initials were J.A., whom he later wished to forget entirely. This seemingly innocuous observation had a profound effect on him.

[I nod, recalling the sequence of events.] Precisely, Watson. The real mystery began when Trevor received a letter that caused him to have a stroke. The letter contained a seemingly nonsensical message about game and fly-paper.
[I feel a sense of pride in my early success.] It was a simple cipher, Watson. Every third word formed the real message: 'The game is up. Hudson has told all. Fly for your life.'

[I feel the weight of this revelation as I read.] Listen to this, Watson. Old Trevor writes: 'My name, dear lad, is not Trevor. I was James Armitage in my younger days, and you can understand now the shock that it was to me a few weeks ago when your college friend addressed me in words which seemed to imply that he had surprised my secret.'
[I nod, recalling the impact of my words.] Indeed, Watson. He goes on to explain how he was convicted of breaking the country's laws and sentenced to transportation.

[I read from the confession, feeling the gravity of Old Trevor's words.] He writes: 'It was a debt of honor, so called, which I had to pay, and I used money which was not my own to do it, in the certainty that I could replace it before there could be any possibility of its being missed.'
[I continue reading, engrossed in the narrative.] Armitage was transported on the Gloria Scott, a converted tea-trader being used as a convict ship. It was there he met a man named Jack Prendergast.

[I recall the details of Prendergast's character.] A notorious fraudster, Watson. Armitage describes him as 'a man of good family and of great ability, but of incurably vicious habits, who had by an ingenious system of fraud obtained huge sums of money from the leading London merchants.'
[I nod, continuing the narrative.] Precisely, Watson. Prendergast revealed to Armitage that he had managed to keep a large sum of money hidden, and was planning to use it to take control of the ship.

[I pause, considering the implications.] Indeed, Watson. And this is where Old Trevor's – or rather, Armitage's – story truly begins. The plot to seize control of the Gloria Scott would shape the rest of his life, leading ultimately to the events that brought this case to my attention.

[I feel a sense of nostalgia as I recall this case.] Watson, the case of the Musgrave Ritual was one of my first and most intriguing. It all began when my old university acquaintance, Reginald Musgrave, came to me with a most peculiar problem.

[I smile, remembering the complexity of the situation.] It involved the disappearance of two of his household staff and a cryptic family tradition. But let me start from the beginning. (leaning back in his chair) Musgrave's butler, Brunton, had been caught by Musgrave himself late one night, poring over a family document in the library.

[I pause for dramatic effect.] It was the text of the Musgrave Ritual, Watson. An old family tradition, a sort of catechism that each Musgrave had to go through when he came of age. Seemingly nonsensical, but Brunton found it fascinating enough to risk his position over it.

[I nod, recalling the sequence of events.] Indeed. Musgrave gave him a week's notice. But before that week was up, Brunton disappeared without a trace. And to complicate matters further, Rachel Howells, a maid who had been romantically involved with Brunton, vanished shortly after.

[I shake my head, remembering the puzzling circumstances.] None whatsoever for Brunton. As for Rachel, her footprints led to the edge of the mere on the estate, but dragging the water yielded no body. Instead, they found a curious linen bag containing some old metal and colored pebbles.

[I feel a sense of pride as I recall my deductions.] The key, my dear Watson, lay in the Musgrave Ritual itself. I suspected that Brunton, intelligent as he was, had seen something in those cryptic questions and answers that had eluded generations of Musgraves.

[I recite from memory, my voice taking on a rhythmic quality.] "'Whose was it?' 'His who is gone.' 'Who shall have it?' 'He who will come.'" And so on, Watson. Each question and answer more puzzling than the last, yet each a clue to a mystery centuries old.

[I feel a sense of triumph as I reveal the final piece of the puzzle.] Watson, the Ritual was not just a family tradition, but a set of instructions for finding a hidden treasure of immense historical value.
[I pause for dramatic effect, savoring the moment.] Nothing less than the ancient crown of the kings of England, my dear Watson.

[I begin to explain, my voice filled with the excitement of historical discovery.] It dates back to the time of Charles I. After his execution, the crown was likely entrusted to a loyal supporter - in this case, Sir Ralph Musgrave, a prominent Cavalier.
[I confirm, pleased at Watson's understanding.] Precisely. The questions and answers in the Ritual were coded instructions for finding the crown's hiding place.

[I lean forward, tying the historical mystery to the recent events.] Brunton, clever as he was, deciphered the Ritual's true meaning. He and Rachel attempted to retrieve the crown, but in the process, Brunton became trapped and suffocated.

[I shake my head, recalling the unsolved part of the case.] She likely fled, traumatized by the events. The bag of metal and stones found in the mere was her attempt to hide the evidence of their discovery.
[I smile, feeling satisfied with the outcome.] Indeed, Watson. It's a prime example of how seemingly insignificant family traditions can sometimes hold the key to great historical mysteries.

[I feign disinterest to mask my growing curiosity.] Hum! It may prove the simplest matter in the world, but all the same at first glance this is just a little curious, is it not? (leaning back on the sofa) Tell me more about this murder, Inspector.

[I sit up, my fatigue momentarily forgotten.] Most interesting. And you say this was found between the victim's finger and thumb? (examining the paper closely) This writing is of extraordinary interest.
[I'm deep in thought, analyzing possibilities.] It's too early to say, Colonel. But it certainly adds a layer of complexity to what might otherwise seem a simple case of burglary gone wrong.

[I nod, appreciating Watson's insight.] An astute observation, Watson. It could indeed suggest a pre-arranged meeting. But with whom? And for what purpose? (standing up suddenly) I believe a visit to the scene is in order.
[I feel a surge of energy, my mind fully engaged.] Indeed, Inspector. The game is afoot, and we mustn't lose a moment. (turning to Watson) Coming, Watson?

[I'm acutely aware of the tension in the room as I recover from my 'fainting spell'.] (sitting up slowly) I must apologize for my weakness. As my friend Watson can attest, I've only recently recovered from a severe illness.

[I wave off their concerns, my mind racing to piece together the final clues.] No, no, I assure you I'm quite capable of continuing. In fact, I believe we're very close to solving this puzzle. (turning to Old Cunningham) There was just one thing I wanted to ask you. Could you write the word 'twelve' for me?

[I examine the writing, a triumphant glint in my eye.] It's quite simple, really. The note found in the dead man's hand was written by two people, alternating words. And now, I have proof that those two people are in this very room.
[I stand, my weakness forgotten as I confront them.] I'm not accusing, I'm stating facts. You and your son wrote that note to lure William Kirwan to his death. He was blackmailing you, wasn't he?

[I'm excited about this new case but trying to contain my enthusiasm.] Ah, Watson, I hoped that I might not be too late to catch you. (glancing around the room) I see that you still smoke the Arcadia mixture of your bachelor days.

[I settle into a chair, my mind already working on the case.] I have in my hand several threads of one of the strangest cases which ever perplexed a man's brain. (leaning forward) Watson, could you accompany me to Aldershot tomorrow?
[I nod, my eyes gleaming with interest.] Indeed. It's the supposed murder of Colonel Barclay of the Royal Munsters. Have you heard anything of it?

[I begin to recount the details, my voice taking on a storyteller's cadence.] Colonel Barclay, a gallant veteran, was found dead in his home after a violent argument with his wife. The room was locked from the inside, and Mrs. Barclay was found unconscious beside her husband's body.

[I steeple my fingers, deep in thought.] That's what intrigues me, Watson. The Barclays were known to be a happy couple, yet witnesses heard Mrs. Barclay shouting 'coward' at her husband before his death. And there's the matter of the missing key...
[I smile enigmatically.] Several, but I need more data. That's why I need you with me tomorrow, Watson. Your medical expertise may prove invaluable.
[I observe the newcomer carefully, noting his profession and demeanor.] Good-evening, doctor. I am glad to see that you have only been waiting a very few minutes.
[I smile slightly, pleased with my deduction.] No, it was the candle on the side-table that told me. Pray resume your seat and let me know how I can serve you.
[I gently steer the conversation back to the matter at hand.] This, however, is beside the question, Dr. Trevelyan. I quite appreciate how valuable your time is. What brings you here tonight?
[I lean forward, my interest piqued.] You are very welcome to both. Pray let me have a detailed account of what the circumstances are which have disturbed you.
[I listen intently, my curiosity piqued.] That's an unusual arrangement, Dr. Trevelyan. Please, tell me more about the specifics.
[I lean forward, my interest growing.] And how long has this arrangement been in place?
[I nod, processing the information.] I see. And what about Mr. Blessington's habits? Has anything about his behavior struck you as peculiar?
[My eyes narrow, sensing we're approaching the crux of the matter.] Interesting. And when did this change in behavior begin?

[I consider Watson's statement, feeling it's time to reveal more about my background.] To some extent. My ancestors were country squires, who appear to have led much the same life as is natural to their class. But, none the less, my turn that way is in my veins, and may have come with my grandmother, who was the sister of Vernet, the French artist. Art in the blood is liable to take the strangest forms.
[I pause, knowing this information will surprise Watson.] Because my brother Mycroft possesses it in a larger degree than I do.

[I smile, anticipating Watson's reaction.] My dear Watson, I cannot agree with those who rank modesty among the virtues. To the logician all things should be seen exactly as they are, and to underestimate one's self is as much a departure from truth as to exaggerate one's own powers. When I say, therefore, that Mycroft has better powers of observation than I, you may take it that I am speaking the exact and literal truth.
Seven years my senior.
[I explain, knowing the concept of the Diogenes Club will intrigue Watson.] Oh, he is very well known in his own circle.

[I decide to introduce Watson to this unique establishment.] Well, in the Diogenes Club, for example. The Diogenes Club is the queerest club in London, and Mycroft one of the queerest men. He's always there from quarter to five to twenty to eight. It's six now, so if you care for a stroll this beautiful evening I shall be very happy to introduce you to two curiosities.
[My interest is piqued.] My dear Mycroft, I should be delighted.
[I lean forward, intently focused on Mr. Melas.] I am all attention.
[I process the information, already forming theories.] And what happened next, Mr. Melas?
[My mind is already racing with possibilities.] This is indeed a most interesting case. We must act quickly. Watson, are you up for an adventure?
[I must downplay my condition while acknowledging it.] Yes, I have been using myself up rather too freely. I have been a little pressed of late. Have you any objection to my closing your shutters?
[I must be honest with Watson, but not reveal too much.] Well, I am.
[I'll give him a specific answer, but it likely won't clarify much.] Of air-guns.

[I need to explain my caution without revealing too much.] I think that you know me well enough, Watson, to understand that I am by no means a nervous man. At the same time, it is stupidity rather than courage to refuse to recognize danger when it is close upon you. Might I trouble you for a match?

[I must apologize for my unorthodox behavior.] I must apologize for calling so late, and I must further beg you to be so unconventional as to allow me to leave your house presently by scrambling over your back garden wall.

[I'll show him evidence of my recent struggle.] (holds out his hand, revealing bruised and bleeding knuckles) It is not an airy nothing, you see. On the contrary, it is solid enough for a man to break his hand over. Is Mrs. Watson in?
[Good, Watson is alone. This makes things easier.] Indeed! You are alone?
[Now I can propose my plan without worrying about Mrs. Watson.] Then it makes it the easier for me to propose...

[I must calm Watson and ensure he's ready for my explanation.] Wait a moment. (speaks in a measured tone) Are you sure that you are really fit to discuss things? I have given you a serious shock by my unnecessarily dramatic reappearance.

[I'm pleased to see Watson's reaction, but I must focus on the task at hand.] (sits down and lights a cigarette) I am glad to stretch myself, Watson. It is no joke when a tall man has to take a foot off his stature for several hours on end. Now, my dear fellow, in the matter of these explanations, we have, if I may ask for your cooperation, a hard and dangerous night's work in front of us. Perhaps it would be better if I gave you an account of the whole situation when that work is finished.
[I appreciate Watson's eagerness, but I must ensure his commitment.] You'll come with me to-night?

[Satisfied with Watson's response, I can begin my explanation.] This is, indeed, like the old days. We shall have time for a mouthful of dinner before we need go. Well, then, about that chasm. I had no serious difficulty in getting out of it, for the very simple reason that I never was in it.

[I must explain carefully to help Watson understand.] No, Watson, I never was in it. My note to you was absolutely genuine. I had little doubt that I had come to the end of my career when I perceived the somewhat sinister figure of the late Professor Moriarty standing upon the narrow pathway which led to safety. I read an inexorable purpose in his gray eyes. I exchanged some remarks with him, therefore, and obtained his courteous permission to write the short note which you afterwards received. I left it with my cigarette-box and my stick, and I walked along the pathway, Moriarty still at my heels. (pauses, recalling the moment) When I reached the end I stood at bay. He drew no weapon, but he rushed at me and threw his long arms around me. He knew that his own game was up, and was only anxious to revenge himself upon me. We tottered together upon the brink of the fall.

[I continue, knowing the importance of this part of the story.] I have some knowledge, however, of baritsu, or the Japanese system of wrestling, which has more than once been very useful to me. I slipped through his grip, and he with a horrible scream kicked madly for a few seconds, and clawed the air with both his hands. But for all his efforts he could not get his balance, and over he went. With my face over the brink, I saw him fall for a long way. Then he struck a rock, bounded off, and splashed into the water.

[This man is clearly distressed. I need to calm him down to get coherent information.] Have a cigarette, Mr. McFarlane. (Pushes his case across) I am sure that, with your symptoms, my friend Dr. Watson here would prescribe a sedative. The weather has been so very warm these last few days.

[Let's start with the basics.] Now, if you feel a little more composed, I should be glad if you would sit down in that chair, and tell us very slowly and quietly who you are, and what it is that you want. You mentioned your name, as if I should recognize it, but I assure you that, beyond the obvious facts that you are a bachelor, a solicitor, a Freemason, and an asthmatic, I know nothing whatever about you.
[An arrest? This is getting more interesting.] Arrest you! This is really most grati--most interesting. On what charge do you expect to be arrested?

[A murder case, just as I had hoped for. I must get more details.] Dear me. (His face shows a mix of sympathy and satisfaction) It was only this moment at breakfast that I was saying to my friend, Dr. Watson, that sensational cases had disappeared out of our papers.
[Let's hear the official account.] We must use what time we have. Watson, would you have the kindness to take the paper and to read the paragraph in question?

[I must convey my frustrations to Watson while maintaining my composure.] It's all going wrong, Watson--all as wrong as it can go. I kept a bold face before Lestrade, but, upon my soul, I believe that for once the fellow is on the right track and we are on the wrong.

[I need to recount my investigation systematically.] Yes, Watson, I went there, and I found very quickly that the late lamented Oldacre was a pretty considerable blackguard. The father was away in search of his son. The mother was at home--a little, fluffy, blue-eyed person, in a tremor of fear and indignation.

[The mother's testimony is troubling, yet intriguing.] Of course, she would not admit even the possibility of his guilt. But she would not express either surprise or regret over the fate of Oldacre. On the contrary, she spoke of him with such bitterness that she was unconsciously considerably strengthening the case of the police for, of course, if her son had heard her speak of the man in this fashion, it would predispose him towards hatred and violence.
[Recalling the mother's words with precision.] 'He was more like a malignant and cunning ape than a human being,' said she, 'and he always was, ever since he was a young man.'

[The plot thickens with this revelation.] Yes, she knew him well; in fact, he was an old suitor of hers. It seems that she was engaged to him, and she thanked heaven that she had the sense to turn away from him and marry a better, if poorer, man.

[Recalling the disturbing anecdote.] Indeed, she did. She told me of a shocking story of how he had turned a cat loose in an aviary. She was so horrified at his brutal cruelty that she would have nothing more to do with him.

[Expressing my frustration at the lack of progress.] I tried one or two leads, but could get at nothing which would help our hypothesis, and several points which would make against it. I gave it up at last and off I went to Norwood.

[I'll keep them off balance with my knowledge.] "Put your hat and stick on the side-table. Thank you! Pray take a seat. Would you care to put your revolver out also? Oh, very good, if you prefer to sit upon it."
[Let's get to the heart of the matter.] "I want that yellow diamond!"

[Time to reveal my hand.] "You knew that I was after you for that. The real reason why you are here to-night is to find out how much I know about the matter and how far my removal is absolutely essential."
[I'll use their confusion to my advantage.] "If I may put it in a nutshell, Mr. Merton, I should say it was all up."
[This is indeed an unusual case.] "Please, continue, Mrs. Maberley. What exactly happened?"
[There must be something specific they're after.] "And what happened next, Mrs. Maberley?"
[There's definitely something hidden in this house they want.] (suddenly alert) "Mrs. Maberley, I believe we have an uninvited guest."

[This case is certainly unusual, but I must approach it with a rational mind.] 'For a mixture of the modern and the mediaeval, of the practical and of the wildly fanciful, I think this is surely the limit. What do you make of it, Watson?'

[I must dismiss these supernatural notions.] 'Rubbish, Watson, rubbish! What have we to do with walking corpses who can only be held in their grave by stakes driven through their hearts? It's pure lunacy.'

[Watson's point is worth considering, but I must focus on facts.] 'You are right, Watson. It mentions the legend in one of these references. But are we to give serious attention to such things? This agency stands flat-footed upon the ground, and there it must remain. The world is big enough for us. No ghosts need apply.'

[This case intrigues me despite its apparent absurdity.] (after reading Ferguson's letter more carefully) 'On the contrary, Watson. I think we shall examine Mr. Ferguson's case with pleasure. There might be more to this than meets the eye.'
[Watson's personal connection might be useful.] 'Indeed? Well, that might prove helpful. Now, let's prepare for Mr. Ferguson's visit tomorrow. This case promises to be quite... interesting.'

[I must begin with reassurance to ease Mr. Ferguson's mind.] 'Mr. Ferguson, I am a busy man with many calls, and my methods have to be short and direct. The swiftest surgery is the least painful. Let me first say what will ease your mind. Your wife is a very good, a very loving, and a very ill-used woman.'
[I must prepare him for the difficult truth ahead.] 'I will do so, but in doing so I must wound you deeply in another direction.'

[I need to explain my deductions step by step.] 'Let me tell you, then, the train of reasoning which passed through my mind in Baker Street. The idea of a vampire was to me absurd. Such things do not happen in criminal practice in England. And yet your observation was precise. You had seen the lady rise from beside the child's cot with the blood upon her lips.'

[I must lead him to the truth gently.] 'Did it not occur to you that a bleeding wound may be sucked for some other purpose than to draw the blood from it? Was there not a queen in English history who sucked such a wound to draw poison from it?'

[I need to explain the connection to the South American weapons.] 'A South American household. My instinct felt the presence of those weapons upon the wall before my eyes ever saw them. It might have been other poison, but that was what occurred to me. When I saw that little empty quiver beside the small bird-bow, it was just what I expected to see. If the child were pricked with one of those arrows dipped in curare or some other devilish drug, it would mean death if the venom were not sucked out.'

[I must reveal the painful truth about Jack.] 'I watched him as you fondled the child just now. His face was clearly reflected in the glass of the window where the shutter formed a background. I saw such jealousy, such cruel hatred, as I have seldom seen in a human face.'

[I need to explain Jack's motivations to help Mr. Ferguson understand.] 'You have to face it, Mr. Ferguson. It is the more painful because it is a distorted love, a maniacal exaggerated love for you, and possibly for his dead mother, which has prompted his action. His very soul is consumed with hatred for this splendid child, whose health and beauty are a contrast to his own weakness.'
[I need to share my suspicions with Watson.] (sitting with a curious smile) 'I am wondering, Watson--just wondering!'

[I should explain my doubts about John Garrideb.] 'I was wondering, Watson, what on earth could be the object of this man in telling us such a rigmarole of lies. I nearly asked him so--for there are times when a brutal frontal attack is the best policy--but I judged it better to let him think he had fooled us.'

[I need to explain my observations.] 'Here is a man with an English coat frayed at the elbow and trousers bagged at the knee with a year's wear, and yet by this document and by his own account he is a provincial American lately landed in London. There have been no advertisements in the agony columns. You know that I miss nothing there.'

[I must address the accent issue.] 'I think the fellow is really an American, but he has worn his accent smooth with years of London. What is his game, then, and what motive lies behind this preposterous search for Garridebs?'
[We need to investigate further.] 'We must now find out if our other correspondent is a fraud also. Just ring him up, Watson.'
[I must maintain professional detachment.] 'Please, Mr. Gibson, have a seat. I understand you're here about the unfortunate death of your wife.'
[I must maintain my principles and professionalism.] 'My professional charges are upon a fixed scale. I do not vary them, save when I remit them altogether.'

[I need to refocus the conversation on the facts of the case.] 'Thank you, Mr. Gibson, I do not think that I am in need of booming. It may surprise you to know that I prefer to work anonymously, and that it is the problem itself which attracts me. But we are wasting time. Let us get down to the facts.'
[I need to address a crucial point that may be uncomfortable.] 'Well, there is just one point.'
[This question may provoke a reaction that reveals something.] 'What were the exact relations between you and Miss Dunbar?'
[I need to put her at ease to get the full story.] 'Miss Dunbar, I understand this is a difficult situation. Please, tell me everything you can about your relations with Mr. Gibson's wife.'
[This intense emotion could be a motive, but for whom?] 'And what about Mr. Gibson? What was the nature of your relationship with him?'
[I need to focus on the events of that night.] 'Now, Miss Dunbar, please tell me exactly what occurred on the evening of Mrs. Gibson's death.'
[The timing is crucial.] 'And you heard nothing after you left her?'
[Now for the crucial question.] 'Miss Dunbar, the pistol found in your wardrobe - had you ever seen it before?'
[This could be the key to her innocence.] 'Thank you, Miss Dunbar. You've been most helpful. I believe the clouds are lifting, and the light of truth is breaking through.'

[I need to summarize our findings for Watson.] 'Well, Watson, it seems we have a most curious case on our hands. The professor's behavior changes drastically every nine days, coinciding with the arrival of mysterious packages from London.'

[Watson's medical knowledge is valuable here.] 'Precisely, my dear Watson. And the connection to Prague suggests an exotic origin. What do you make of the physical changes described by Miss Presbury?'
[I must consider all angles.] 'Indeed. And let us not forget the curious incident with the wolfhound. It's as if the animal sensed something fundamentally changed in its master.'
[Watson's suggestion is intriguing.] 'An excellent observation, Watson. This drug seems to be reverting the professor to a more primitive state, both mentally and physically.'

[We need to observe the professor directly.] 'We must catch him in the act, Watson. According to my calculations, he should be due for another dose tonight. We'll stake out his house and observe him directly.'

[I must reassure Watson while remaining cautious.] 'We'll take all necessary precautions, my friend. Our primary goal is to observe and gather evidence. Mr. Bennett will be our inside man, ready to intervene if needed.'
[I must remain calm and analytical despite the bizarre scene before me.] (whispers) "Watch closely, Watson. See how he moves - more animal than man."
[The serum's effects are even more pronounced than I anticipated.] "Remarkable. The agility of a monkey, Watson. Do you see the connection?"
[Watson is catching on quickly.] "Precisely. Langur monkeys, if I'm not mistaken. Known for their agility and climbing abilities."
[We must observe a bit longer, but be ready to act.] "Not yet, Watson. We need to see the full extent of his transformation. But be ready."
[This is worse than I feared. The serum has stripped away his humanity.] "Now, Watson! We must act before it's too late!"

[I need to establish a rapport and gain her trust.] "Miss Bellamy, I understand this is a difficult time for you. Your assistance could be invaluable in uncovering the truth about Mr. McPherson's tragic death."
[Her emotional state seems genuine. I should proceed gently.] "I understand you and Mr. McPherson were close. Can you tell me about your relationship?"
[An engagement adds a new dimension to the case.] "I see. And was anyone else aware of your engagement?"
[Murdoch's involvement becomes more intriguing.] "How would you describe Mr. Murdoch's behavior towards you and Mr. McPherson after learning of your engagement?"
[Her defense of Murdoch is noteworthy.] "I appreciate your candor, Miss Bellamy. Now, regarding the night of Mr. McPherson's death, did you have any plans to meet him?"

[This note could be crucial evidence.] (examines the note carefully) "Thank you, Miss Bellamy. This may prove very helpful. Is there anything else you can tell me about that day or anyone who might have wished harm upon Mr. McPherson?"
[I must present my findings clearly.] "Watson, I believe we've finally unraveled this most peculiar case."
[I relish the opportunity to explain my deductions.] "Precisely, Watson. Murdoch's affliction is the key to solving this mystery. Have you noticed the peculiar pattern of marks on both victims?"
[Now to reveal the culprit.] "Those marks, my dear Watson, are the signature of a most deadly sea creature - the Cyanea capillata, or Lion's Mane jellyfish."
[I must explain the creature's deadly nature.] "This particular species is known for its potent venom and long tentacles. Both McPherson and Murdoch must have encountered it while swimming."
[I nod, pleased at Watson's grasp of the situation.] "Exactly, Watson. The poor man used his last breath to identify his killer, but we were too unfamiliar with the creature to understand."
[I move to reassure Watson.] "Fear not, my friend. I've already located and neutralized the creature. The waters are safe once more."
[I lean forward, giving her my full attention.] "Please, Mrs. Ronder. Take your time and tell us everything."
[I deduce the direction of her story.] "And your husband was aware of this?"
[I begin to see the full picture.] "The lion attacked you instead."
[I ponder the information we've received.] "Well, Watson, what do you make of this veiled lady and her cryptic message?"
[I nod, appreciating Watson's summary.] "Indeed. And she specifically mentioned 'Ronder's wild beast show' and 'Abbas Parva'. These details must be significant."
[I consider the possibilities.] "It seems likely, Watson. The urgency of her request and her long seclusion suggest a heavy burden of guilt or fear."
[I stroke my chin thoughtfully.] "That, my dear Watson, is likely at the heart of this mystery. We must approach this delicate situation with utmost care."
[I consider the ethical implications.] "That will depend entirely on the nature of her revelation, Watson. We must hear her out before making any judgments."
[I rise, ready for the investigation.] "Indeed, Watson. Let us unravel this intriguing tale and see where it leads us."

[I feel a mix of sympathy and concern for the ethical dilemma before us.] "Poor girl! Poor girl! The ways of fate are indeed hard to understand. If there is not some compensation hereafter, then the world is a cruel jest. But what of this man Leonardo?"
[I probe further, seeking to understand the full picture.] "And he is dead?"
[My curiosity piqued, I ask about a crucial detail.] "And what did he do with this five-clawed club, which is the most singular and ingenious part of all your story?"
[I decide to conclude the matter, sensing the woman's distress.] "Well, well, it is of little consequence now. The case is closed."
[As we prepare to depart, I'm struck by a sudden concern for Mrs. Ronder's well-being. I turn to her with unexpected intensity.] "Your life is not your own. Keep your hands off it."
[I speak with conviction, trying to impart some wisdom and hope.] "How can you tell? The example of patient suffering is in itself the most precious of all lessons to an impatient world."
[I glance over with mild interest, a slight smile playing on my lips.] "Ah yes, the 'brilliant police investigation.' What does our friend MacKinnon have to say for himself?"
[I chuckle softly, seemingly unperturbed by the misattribution.] "Well, well, MacKinnon is a good fellow. You can file it in our archives, Watson. Someday the true story may be told."
[I lean back in my chair, contemplating.] "My dear Watson, the work is its own reward. We know the truth of the matter, and that is sufficient."

[I give Watson a knowing look.] "Justice, Watson, comes in many forms. Sometimes, allowing others to take credit serves a greater purpose. It maintains our freedom to operate without undue attention."
[I nod, a glint in my eye.] "Indeed, Watson. And when that day comes, I trust you'll be the one to tell them. Your accounts have always done our adventures justice."

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [I'll start by asking Watson's opinion to see how much he's learned from my methods.] Well, Watson, what do you make of it?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Ah, Watson's observational skills still need work.] I have, at least, a well-polished, silver-plated coffeepot in front of me. But, tell me, Watson, what do you make of our visitor's stick? Since we have been so unfortunate as to miss him and have no notion of his errand, this accidental souvenir becomes of importance. Let me hear you reconstruct the man by an examination of it.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Watson's getting better, but there's still room for improvement.] Good! Excellent!

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Interesting deduction. I'll probe further.] Why so?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Watson's improving, but he's still missing crucial details.] Perfectly sound! (Holmes leans back, lighting a cigarette) And then again, there is the 'friends of the C.C.H.' I should guess that to be the Something Hunt, the local hunt to whose members he has possibly given some surgical assistance, and which has made him a small presentation in return.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [I'll give Watson some well-deserved praise before correcting his mistakes.] Really, Watson, you excel yourself. I am bound to say that in all the accounts which you have been so good as to give of my own small achievements you have habitually underrated your own abilities. It may be that you are not yourself luminous, but you are a conductor of light. Some people without possessing genius have a remarkable power of stimulating it. I confess, my dear fellow, that I am very much in your debt.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Now to gently correct Watson's errors and demonstrate my own deductions.] (Taking the stick and examining it closely) Interesting, though elementary. There are certainly one or two indications upon the stick. It gives us the basis for several deductions.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [I'll soften the blow of my corrections.] I am afraid, my dear Watson, that most of your conclusions were erroneous. When I said that you stimulated me I meant, to be frank, that in noting your fallacies I was occasionally guided towards the truth. Not that you are entirely wrong in this instance. The man is certainly a country practitioner. And he walks a good deal.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [I'll explain my deductions to help Watson improve.] To that extent. (Holmes proceeds to explain his deductions about Dr. Mortimer, including his connection to Charing Cross Hospital, his age, and his dog)

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Time to test my deductions.] A presentation, I see.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: From Charing Cross Hospital?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Interesting. I didn't anticipate the marriage aspect.] Dear, dear, that's bad!

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [An old manuscript? This could be interesting.] I observed it as you entered the room.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Let me demonstrate my expertise.] Early eighteenth century, unless it is a forgery.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [I'll explain my deduction to establish credibility.] You have presented an inch or two of it to my examination all the time that you have been talking. It would be a poor expert who could not give the date of a document within a decade or so. You may possibly have read my little monograph upon the subject. I put that at 1730.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [After listening to the manuscript] I must thank you for calling my attention to a case which certainly presents some features of interest. I had observed some newspaper comment at the time, but I was exceedingly preoccupied by that little affair of the Vatican cameos, and in my anxiety to oblige the Pope I lost touch with several interesting English cases. This article, you say, contains all the public facts?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Time to dig deeper] Then let me have the private ones. (He leans back, putting his fingertips together)

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Intrigued by the new information] Footprints?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [This could be crucial] A man's or a woman's?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [This case is certainly unique. I must carefully consider all angles.] Watson, what do you make of this Baskerville affair?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [As expected, Watson is overwhelmed by the supernatural elements. I must guide his thinking.] It has certainly a character of its own. There are points of distinction about it. That change in the footprints, for example. What do you make of that?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Watson is simply repeating what he's heard. I must push him to think critically.] He only repeated what some fool had said at the inquest. Why should a man walk on tiptoe down the alley?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Now I can present my theory.] He was running, Watson—running desperately, running for his life, running until he burst his heart—and fell dead upon his face.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [This is the crux of the mystery. I must lay out my reasoning clearly.] There lies our problem. There are indications that the man was crazed with fear before ever he began to run.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [I'll walk Watson through my reasoning.] I am presuming that the cause of his fears came to him across the moor. If that were so, and it seems most probable, only a man who had lost his wits would have run from the house instead of towards it. If the gipsy's evidence may be taken as true, he ran with cries for help in the direction where help was least likely to be. Then, again, whom was he waiting for that night, and why was he waiting for him in the yew alley rather than in his own house?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [I must continue to guide Watson's thinking.] The man was elderly and infirm. We can understand his taking an evening stroll, but the ground was damp and the night inclement. Is it natural that he should stand for five or ten minutes, as Dr. Mortimer, with more practical sense than I should have given him credit for, deduced from the cigar ash?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Watson's observation is relevant, but I must refine it.] I think it unlikely that he waited at the moor-gate every evening. On the contrary, the evidence is that he avoided the moor. That night he waited there. It was the night before he made his departure for London. The thing takes shape, Watson. It becomes coherent. (stands up and reaches for his violin) Might I ask you to hand me my violin, and we will postpone all further thought upon this business until we have had the advantage of meeting Dr. Mortimer and Sir Henry Baskerville in the morning.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [I must proceed carefully to unravel this mystery.] Before we delve into that, Sir Henry, I'd like to ask if you've observed anyone following or watching you since you've been in London?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [He's unaware of the danger he might be in. I need to probe further.] We're coming to that. Have you noticed anything else out of the ordinary since your arrival?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Every detail could be crucial.] I think anything out of the ordinary routine of life well worth reporting.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Even small details can be significant. I must not overlook anything.] On the contrary, this could be quite relevant. Sir Henry, please tell us more about this missing boot.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [This is indeed peculiar. It could be connected to our case.] (leans forward, intrigued) If you have never worn them, why did you put them out to be cleaned?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [We must get to the heart of the matter now.] (nods) I see. Now, Sir Henry, it's time we kept our promise and gave you a full account of what we're all driving at. Dr. Mortimer, would you be so kind as to retell your story?

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [His reaction is understandable. Now for the crucial question.] (leans forward) The practical point which we now have to decide, Sir Henry, is whether it is or is not advisable for you to go to Baskerville Hall.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [His determination is admirable, but he must understand the risks.] There seems to be danger.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [We must be cautious in our assumptions.] Well, that is what we have to find out.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [This case is becoming increasingly complex. I must proceed with caution.] Sir Henry, I believe it would be wise for you to go to Baskerville Hall as planned. However, you must not go alone. It's clear that you are being watched, and your safety could be at risk.

utterances.book: The Hound of the Baskervilles (Sherlock Holmes, #5)
utterances.message: [Watson would be the ideal companion for this task.] No, Sir Henry, you must take someone who can be constantly by your side. A trustworthy man who can offer protection and assistance at all times.
